Current EoE treatment strategies aim to suppress esophageal inflammation and prevent long-term complications. To date, three pharmacologic agents have been approved: dupilumab ( 4 ) and two oral formulations of budesonide ( 5 , 6 ). Advances in our understanding of EoE immunopathogenesis have enabled the development of targeted biologic therapies that modulate key mediators of type 2 inflammation. These include monoclonal antibodies directed against the interleukin (IL)-4 receptor alpha (dupilumab) ( 7 , 8 ); IL-13 (cendakimab) ( 9 , 10 ); IL-5 (mepolizumab, reslizumab) ( 11 , 12 ); and the IL-5 receptor (benralizumab) ( 13 ). Additional investigational agents include lirentelimab, an anti-Siglec-8 monoclonal antibody that selectively depletes eosinophils ( 14 ), and etrasimod, an oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator that impairs lymphocyte trafficking to inflamed tissues ( 15 ).

A prior network meta-analysis (NMA) focused largely on histologic endpoints across the available pharmacologic therapies. Most corticosteroid studies included in this review followed patients for 6–8 weeks (with a few extending to 12 weeks), whereas many biologic trials reported outcomes at 12 or 24 weeks. Because outcomes were not uniformly stratified by time point, aligning comparisons across interventions was challenging and may have contributed to variability in the findings ( 16 ).

To address these limitations, we conducted a comparative analysis of individual biologic agents, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and corticosteroids at 12, 24, and 48 weeks, focusing on key EoE outcomes—reduction of dysphagia and histological remission, as well as improvement in endoscopic appearance measured by the Eosinophilic Esophagitis Endoscopic Reference Score (EREFS). Our analyses are intended to inform clinical decision-making and optimize treatment strategies for patients with EoE. The certainty of evidence across all treatment comparisons was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework adapted for network meta-analysis ( 17 ).

Methods Protocol and Registration We adhered to the network version of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, which provide a standardized framework for reporting the methodology and findings of systematic reviews and network meta-analyses ( 18 ) ( Supplementary File ). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO under CRD420261281588.

Literature Search We systematically searched the PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases from inception to May 25, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that met the predefined eligibility criteria. To ensure the search remained current prior to manuscript submission, an updated search was performed in January 2026 using the same search strategy and eligibility criteria.

In addition, we conducted manual screening of ongoing and unpublished trials on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Our search strategy incorporated key terms related to “EoE,” “steroid medications,” “PPI,” “biological therapy,” and “monoclonal antibodies” ( eTable S1 ).

Eligibility Criteria and Study Selection Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of studies that met the inclusion criteria. Eligible studies were RCTs enrolling adolescents or adults (≥12 years) with EoE as per contemporaneous diagnostic criteria, comparing topical/systemic corticosteroids, biologic agents, or PPIs against placebo or another active intervention, with a minimum follow-up of 12 weeks. Ongoing or unpublished trials with results available through conference proceedings, ClinicalTrials.gov , or the WHO ICTRP were also included.

We excluded trials limited to pediatric patients <12 years, studies with follow-up <12 weeks, studies focused on eosinophilic gastritis, studies with overlapping data, and non-randomized studies. Data Extraction and Outcomes Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized Excel form with two sheets. The first captured study and baseline characteristics: author, year, country, trial phase, follow-up duration, study groups (intervention/control), sample size, gender, age, disease duration, prior glucocorticosteroid use, and dysphagia scale.

Key outcomes included changes in dysphagia from baseline and histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils/high-power field [eos/hpf]) at 12, 24, and 48 weeks. Because dysphagia instruments varied (Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire [DSQ], Eosinophilic Esophagitis Activity Index [EEsAI], Dysphagia Symptom Diary [DSD], modified DSD), we calculated standardized mean differences (SMDs). We oriented all scales so that positive values indicated improvement.

Additional outcomes were change in endoscopic features of EoE as measured with the EREFS score at 12, 24, and 48 weeks (EREFS was analyzed as a continuous change score higher values denote worse endoscopic abnormalities; decreases reflect improvement), change in EoE-HSS grade and stage (0–3) at 24 weeks; absolute change in peak eosinophil count at 12 weeks and percentage change in peak eosinophil count at 24 weeks; and histologic response (<15 eos/hpf) at 12, 24, and 48 weeks.

When numerical data were not available in text/tables, we digitized figures using WebPlotDigitizer. If results were reported as least-squares means (LSMs) with standard errors (SEs), we treated LSMs as means and converted SEs to SDs using SD = SE × √n. Where studies reported medians and interquartile ranges, we used standard methods to approximate means and SDs ( 19 ). Assessment for Bias The risk of bias in the included studies was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 (ROB 2.0) ( 20 ). Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with senior authors.

Clinically Meaningful Difference Clinically meaningful differences (CMDs) were defined prospectively to facilitate interpretation of effect estimates and judgments regarding imprecision. Because no validated CMD thresholds exist for EoE, we defined CMD thresholds based on methodological approaches used for synthesis of evidence in recent American Gastroenterological Association guidelines for other chronic autoimmune inflammatory gastrointestinal diseases (ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease) ( 21 , 22 ).

For dichotomous outcomes, we defined CMDs as an absolute risk difference (ARD) ≥10% for placebo-controlled trials and ≥5% for active-comparator trials. Because continuous outcomes were reported using different dysphagia instruments, results were standardized as SMDs and interpreted using Cohen’s criteria (0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 indicating small, moderate, and large effects) ( 23 – 25 ). We defined a clinically meaningful difference as an SMD ≥0.30 in placebo-controlled trials and ≥0.20 in active-comparator trials.

Sensitivity analyses evaluated more conservative thresholds (15% and 10% for dichotomous outcomes and SMD ≥0.50 and ≥0.40 for continuous outcomes in placebo-controlled and active-comparator settings, respectively). GRADE assessment Evidence certainty was assessed using the GRADE framework ( 17 ). Indirect estimates began at the lower certainty of the two direct comparisons forming the initial network loop, with further downgrading for imprecision or intransitivity indicating clinical or methodological heterogeneity. Network consistency, when feasible, was evaluated using node-splitting analyses comparing direct and indirect estimates.

Imprecision was assessed using CMD thresholds. Downgrading was one level if the 95% CI crossed the CMD but not the null; two if it crossed both the null and CMD in one direction; and three if it spanned benefit, no effect, and harm. If no downgrading occurred, the optimal information size (OIS) was evaluated; further downgrading was performed if the upper-to-lower CI ratio exceeded 3. Per GRADE, moderate- and low-certainty evidence were described as “likely” and “possibly” ( 26 ).

Statistical Analysis A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was conducted in R (version 4.2.2) using the netmeta package, following the intention-to-treat principle. Treatment effects were estimated on the log risk ratio (log-RR) scale for dichotomous outcomes. For each treatment serving as the reference in league tables, baseline risk was estimated as the pooled event rate among participants receiving that treatment across all relevant trial arms ( 27 ). ARDs were derived by applying pooled risk ratios to baseline risks using the formula: ARD = BR × (RR – 1) ( 28 ).

For continuous outcomes, SMDs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. The transitivity assumption was evaluated by comparing key clinical and methodological characteristics across treatment comparisons, including age, sex distribution, disease duration, baseline EREFS, prior glucocorticosteroid use, and baseline peak eosinophil count. Network geometry was examined to identify closed loops and assess the feasibility of formal inconsistency testing. Because most trials compared active treatments with placebo and few head-to-head comparisons between active agents were available, the network was largely star-shaped. Closed loops occurred primarily among different dosing regimens of the same agent, limiting formal inconsistency testing between distinct active treatments. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity ( 29 ). Publication bias was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots and formally tested using Egger’s regression test.

Intervention rankings were derived using the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking (SUCRA) curve, with higher values indicating more favorable outcomes. However, SUCRA values should be interpreted alongside the magnitude of effect estimates and their associated uncertainty, rather than in isolation ( 30 ). Conclusions regarding comparative efficacy were based primarily on the effect estimates and their certainty of evidence, with SUCRA rankings presented as supplementary information rather than as the basis for inference.

An arm-based mixed-effects meta-regression was implemented with the metafor package to evaluate the impact of baseline patient characteristics on treatment effects ( 31 ). Within-study dependence among multiple effect sizes was addressed by applying this method ( 32 , 33 ). Covariate selection was guided by clinical relevance and by consistency in reporting across studies. Sex and age were entered as covariates in the model. Result: Studies Characteristics A total of 7,393 records were identified through database searches, of which 12 studies comprising 13 RCTs were included ( 7 – 10 , 12 – 15 , 34 – 37 ), as one study included two separate trials ( Figure 1 ).

Of the 13 included RCTs, 11 were published as full-text articles ( 7 – 9 , 12 , 13 , 15 , 34 – 37 ), while two were completed but unpublished at the time of analysis; however, their final results were available on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04322708 , NCT04753697 ) ( 10 , 14 ). Six trials were Phase III studies ( 7 , 10 , 13 , 34 , 37 ), one was a combined Phase II/III trial ( 14 ), and the remaining six were Phase II trials ( 8 , 9 , 12 , 15 , 35 , 36 ). Among the 13 RCTs included, 11 evaluated induction of remission at 12 or 24 weeks in active EoE ( 7 – 9 , 12 – 15 , 34 – 36 ); one evaluated induction at 24 weeks followed by maintenance at 48 weeks ( 10 ); and one evaluated maintenance of remission alone at 48 weeks ( 37 ).

Overall, the 13 trials enrolled a total of 2,163 participants. The distribution of interventions was as follows: dupilumab 300mg (n = 145), benralizumab 30mg (n = 103), mepolizumab 300mg (n = 32), cendakimab 360mg (n = 320), lirentelimab 1mg/kg (n = 93), lirentelimab 3mg/kg (n = 91), etrasimod 2mg (n = 41), etrasimod 1mg (n = 39), budesonide oral suspension (BOS) 2mg (n = 264), APT-1011 3mg twice daily (BID) (n = 20), APT-1011 3mg horasomni (at bedtime; HS) (n = 21), APT-1011 1.5mg BID (n = 22), APT-1011 1.5 mgHS (n = 21), budesonide orodispersible tablets (BOT) 0.5mg (n=68), BOT 1mg (n=68), and placebo (n = 813) ( eTable S2 ).

Risk of Bias and Publication Bias Two trials were judged at low risk of bias, while eleven raised some concerns ( eFigure S1 ). Egger’s test showed no evidence of publication bias for dysphagia (P=0.25 at 12 weeks; P=0.40 at 24 weeks) or histologic remission (P=0.99 at 12 weeks; P=0.74 at 24 weeks) ( eFigure S2 ).

Improvement in the Dysphagia symptom At 12 weeks, the NMA included 1,676 patients across eight interventions, including placebo ( Figure 2A ). Dupilumab 300mg was associated with a high-certainty improvement in dysphagia compared with placebo, whereas cendakimab 360mg and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit, with SMDs ranging from −0.31 to −0.54 ( eTable S3 ). Dupilumab 300mg also showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefit compared with lirentelimab at both 1mg/kg and 3mg/kg, as well as compared with benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.69, −0.42, and −0.65, respectively. In contrast, cendakimab 360mg and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit only when compared with lirentelimab 1mg/kg and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs ranging from −0.31 to −0.50. The sensitivity analysis indicated that Dupilumab 300mg shifted from high-to moderate-certainty benefit relative to placebo, lirentelimab 1 mg/kg, and benralizumab 30mg ( eTable S4 ).

Direct pairwise comparisons confirmed the superiority of dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg over placebo ( eFigure S2 ). Based on SUCRA, dupilumab 300mg ranked highest in symptomatic efficacy (92%) ( eFigure S6A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%). At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,194 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2B ). Dupilumab 300mg demonstrated a sustained high-certainty benefit, while cendakimab 360mg showed a sustained moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with SMDs of −0.64 and −0.34, respectively ( eTable S5 ).

Dupilumab 300mg also showed high-to moderate-certainty benefit compared with lirentelimab at both 1mg/kg and 3mg/kg, etrasimod 1mg, and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.79, −0.42, −0.56, and −0.78, respectively. In contrast, cendakimab 360mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit only when compared with lirentelimab 1 mg/kg and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.49 and −0.50, respectively. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg relative to placebo was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S6 ).

Direct comparisons confirmed the supcriority of dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg over placebo ( eFigure S4 ). SUCRA again ranked dupilumab 300mg as the most effective treatment (97%) ( eFigure S6B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 470 patients across five interventions ( Figure 2C ). BOT 0.5mg and BOT 1mg were associated with high-certainty improvement in dysphagia compared with placebo, with SMDs of −1.19 and −1.43, respectively. Both doses also demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with cendakimab 360mg administered weekly or every two weeks, with SMDs ranging from −0.89 to −1.17 ( eTable S7 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S8 ).

Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of BOT 0.5mg and 1mg over placebo, while no differences were observed between cendakimab 360mg weekly and every two weeks compared with placebo ( eFigure S5 ). According to SUCRA, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective treatment (96%) ( eFigure S6C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Histological remission At 12 weeks, the NMA included 619 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2D ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 9.05 to 28.76 ( eTable S9 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S10 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S7 ). SUCRA identified BOS 2mg as the most effective intervention (78%) ( eFigure S10A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,212 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2E ). All interventions except etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 8.09 to 13.36 ( eTable S11 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results ( eTable S12 ). Direct comparisons yielded results similar to those of the indirect comparisons ( eFigure S8 ). SUCRA ranked benralizumab 30mg as the most effective intervention (80%) ( eFigure S10B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 498 patients across five interventions ( Figure 2F ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.86 to 8.71 ( eTable S13 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S14 ). Direct comparison results were consistent with the network estimates ( eFigure S9 ). According to SUCRA analysis, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective treatment (79%) ( eFigure S10C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Improvement in EREFS At 12 weeks, the NMA included 619 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S11 ). Dupilumab 300mg and APT-1011 (3mg HS and 1.5 mg BID) yielded high-certainty evidence of benefit, whereas BOS 2mg and APT-1011 (1.5mg HS and 3 mg BID) provided moderate-certainty evidence of benefit relative to placebo, with SMDs between −0.56 and −1.33 ( eTable S15 ). Sensitivity analyses reduced the certainty rating for the benefit of dupilumab 300mg and APT-1011 1.5 mg BID versus placebo from high to moderate ( eTable S16 ). These findings were corroborated by direct pairwise comparisons ( eFigure S12 ). According to SUCRA, APT-1011 3mg HS ranked highest (86%) ( eFigure S15A ). Substantial heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 53.3%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,170 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S11 ). Dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg demonstrated high-certainty evidence of benefit, whereas etrasimod 2mg showed moderate-certainty benefit relative to placebo (SMDs: −1.16, −1.01, and −0.49, respectively) ( eTable S17 ). Dupilumab also demonstrated moderate-to-high certainty benefit over lirentelimab (1mg/kg and 3mg/kg), etrasimod (1mg and 2mg), and benralizumab 30mg (SMDs: −1.21, −1.29, −0.83, −0.66, and −1.10, respectively). Cendakimab 360mg showed moderate-to-high certainty benefit over etrasimod 1mg, lirentelimab (1mg/kg and 3mg/kg), and benralizumab 30 mg (SMDs: −0.68, −1.07, −1.15, and −0.96, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with etrasimod 1mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S18 ). Direct comparisons with placebo supported these results ( eFigure S13 ). Dupilumab 300mg was ranked as the most effective treatment by SUCRA (96%) ( eFigure S15B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 482 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S11 ). All active treatments demonstrated high-certainty evidence of benefit compared with placebo, with SMDs ranging from −0.76 to −1.96 ( eTable S19 ). BOT 0.5mg and 1mg also demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with cendakimab 360mg administered either weekly or every two weeks, with SMDs ranging from −1.18 to – 1.20. Sensitivity analyses reduced the certainty rating for the benefit of cendakimab 360mg once weekly and once every two weeks versus placebo from high to moderate ( eTable S20 ).

Direct comparisons against placebo were consistent with the indirect analysis ( eFigure S14 ). Based on SUCRA rankings, BOT 0.5mg and 1mg were identified as the most effective interventions (88%) ( eFigure S15C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Improvement in EOE-HSS grade score. At 24 weeks, the NMA included 708 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S16A ). Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated high-certainty benefit over placebo, with SMDs ranging from −1.04 to −1.78 ( eTable S21 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit over etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) (SMDs: −0.74 and −0.63, respectively). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S22 ). Direct comparisons with placebo showed similar results ( eFigure S17A ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg highest in efficacy (97%) ( eFigure S18A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

Improvement in the EOE-HSS stage score At 24 weeks, the NMA again included 708 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S16B ). Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated high-certainty improvement relative to placebo, with SMDs ranging from −1.08 to −1.89 ( eTable S23 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated moderate-to-high certainty benefit over cendakimab 360mg and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) (SMDs: −0.47, −0.81, and −0.65, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with etrasimod 1mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S24 ). Direct pairwise comparisons with placebo supported these findings ( eFigure S17B ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg as the most effective treatment (99%) ( eFigure S18B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

Change in peak eosinophilic count At 12 weeks, the NMA included 516 patients across four interventions and assessed absolute change in peak eosinophil count ( eFigure S19A ). Dupilumab 300mg, mepolizumab 300mg, and BOS 2mg demonstrated high-certainty benefits compared with placebo, with SMDs ranging from −0.99 to −2.33 ( eTable S25 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated a high-certainty benefit over mepolizumab 300mg and BOS 2mg (SMDs: −1.19 and −1.24, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with mepolizumab 300mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S26 ). The superiority over placebo was confirmed in direct comparisons ( eFigure S20A ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg highest (100%) ( eFigure S21A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 450 patients across three interventions and assessed percentage change in peak eosinophil count ( eFigure S19B ). Benralizumab 30mg and dupilumab 300mg demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with placebo (SMDs: −1.44 and −1.23, respectively) ( eTable S27 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S28 ). The superiority of these interventions over placebo was confirmed by direct comparisons ( eFigure S20B ). Benralizumab 30mg ranked highest in SUCRA (87%) ( eFigure S21B ). Moderate heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 43.3%).

Histological response At 12 weeks, the NMA included 532 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S22A ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit over placebo, with RRs ranging from 12.67 to 65.07 ( eTable S29 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S30 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S23 ). SUCRA identified BOS 2mg as the most effective intervention (89%) ( eFigure S26A ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,212 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S22B ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.78 to 11.40 ( eTable S31 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded comparable results ( eTable S32 ). Direct comparisons with placebo confirmed these findings ( eFigure S24 ). Cendakimab 360mg was ranked as the most effective intervention (76%) by SUCRA ( eFigure S26B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 498 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S22C ). All treatments showed moderate-certainty benefit over placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.86 to 8.71 ( eTable S33 ). Sensitivity analyses supported the primary findings ( eTable S34 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S25 ). According to SUCRA, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective intervention (79%) ( eFigure S26C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Meta-regression Age and sex were reported in all included studies and were therefore incorporated into the meta-regression analyses. Other potentially relevant variables, including PPI use, corticosteroid treatment, and baseline eosinophil count, were not consistently reported across trials and could not be included in the models. Meta-regression analyses did not identify significant effect modification by male proportion or increasing age for changes in dysphagia symptoms at 12 and 24 weeks, EREFS at 24 weeks, or peak eosinophil count at 12 and 24 weeks. However, increasing age was associated with a greater change in EREFS at 12 weeks ( eTable S35 ).

DISCUSSION In this NMA, we evaluated the comparative efficacy of biologic and swallowed topical steroid therapies in EoE, focusing on clinical, histologic, and endoscopic outcomes at 12, 24, and 48 weeks. Results were available only for BOS, mepolizumab, and APT-1011 at 12 weeks, while data for etrasimod and lirentelimab were available only at 24 weeks. Data were available for dupilumab and benralizumab at both 12 and 24 weeks. Data for cendakimab were available at 12, 24, and 48 weeks, whereas results for BOT were available only at 48 weeks. No RCTs meeting our inclusion criteria for PPIs were identified. The primary outcomes in our NMA, patient symptoms (reduction in dysphagia) and histologic remission, were chosen to be in line with the US Food and Drug Administration guidance on EoE trials. The certainty of evidence for all comparisons was evaluated using the GRADE tool.

In terms of dysphagia reduction, dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-to-high-certainty benefits over placebo. These agents also showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefit and outperformed several active comparators, including benralizumab 30mg and lirentelimab 1mg/kg, with dupilumab 300mg additionally surpassing lirentelimab 3mg/kg and etrasimod 1mg. Conversely, BOT 0.5mg and 1mg showed high-certainty benefit over both cendakimab 360mg and placebo at 48 weeks.

For histologic remission, all agents showed moderate certainty benefit over placebo except etrasimod. All agents, including etrasimod, also demonstrated moderate certainty benefit compared with placebo for the secondary outcome of histologic response. Other secondary histologic outcomes were also examined. Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) were all superior, with moderate certainty, to placebo for both EoE-HS grade and stage scores. Notably, dupilumab 300mg showed moderate certainty benefit and outperformed etrasimod across both doses for grade scores and was superior to both cendakimab and etrasimod across both doses for stage scores.

Reductions in peak eosinophil counts compared to placebo were achieved with dupilumab 300mg, mepolizumab 300mg, BOS 2mg, and benralizumab 30mg, with dupilumab demonstrating greater reductions than both mepolizumab and BOS. All were supported by high certainty evidence. Assessment of endoscopic improvement, as measured by the EREFS, showed that ATP-1011 (all doses), BOS 2mg, dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod 2mg had moderate certainty of benefit and were more effective than placebo. Additionally, dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefits compared with etrasimod 1mg, benralizumab 30mg, and lirentelimab 1mg/kg. Dupilumab 300mg also showed superiority over etrasimod 2 mg.

Taken together, the symptom and endoscopic outcomes highlight dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg as valuable therapeutic options with moderate certainty of benefit for the management of EoE within a 12-week timeframe. All three were also effective in achieving histologic remission and response, while dupilumab 300mg showed superior results in other secondary histologic outcomes, including EoE-HSS and changes in peak eosinophil count. While dupilumab and cendakimab demonstrated sustained efficacy through 24 weeks, the long-term effectiveness of BOS 2mg remains to be established, as all trials with BOS 2mg in our NMA were 12 weeks in duration. On the other hand, BOT (0.5 and Img) showed a high-certainty benefit over cendakimab 360mg and placebo for symptom and endoscopic outcomes at 48 weeks, but only a moderate-certainty benefit over placebo for histologic remission and response at 48 weeks. Of note, short-term BOT treatment was excluded from the comparisons, as its efficacy was assessed following only 6 weeks of induction therapy ( 38 ).

Dupilumab remains the sole biologic therapy approved by the US FDA and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of EoE ( 4 , 39 ), alongside two oral budesonide formulations ( 5 , 6 ). The 2025 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guidelines provide a conditional recommendation for dupilumab in patients aged 12 years and older who remain symptomatic despite PPI therapy, supported by moderate-quality evidence ( 40 ). However, due to limited evidence, the guidelines do not extend their recommendations to other emerging biologic agents currently under investigation.

It is now well established that symptom severity in EoE, particularly dysphagia, does not always correlate with histologic or endoscopic disease activity ( 41 , 42 ). Several explanations have been proposed for this discordance, including the presence of fixed fibrostenotic changes, which may limit symptomatic improvement even when mucosal inflammation is reduced ( 43 ), adaptive eating behaviors that may mask dysphagia ( 44 ), or concomitant oesophageal motility disorders ( 45 , 46 ). Prior esophageal dilation may also influence clinical outcomes independently of histologic response ( 47 , 48 ). Among patients treated with BOS, histologic responses were similar regardless of dilation history; however, those with prior dilation were less likely to achieve symptomatic improvement, while modestly greater improvements in EREFS were observed ( 47 ). These findings suggest that dilation history may reflect underlying fibrostenotic disease and may confound the relationship between symptomatic improvement and anti-inflammatory therapy. However, in the NMA, baseline disease characteristics were well balanced between intervention and placebo groups, making it less likely that differences in initial disease severity account for the observed dissociation between clinical and histologic outcomes.

Another consideration is the limited clinical impact of targeting the IL-5 and Siglec-8 pathways in isolation. While IL-5-directed therapies such as benralizumab and mepolizumab, and Siglec-8-directed therapy such as lirentelimab, effectively reduce tissue eosinophil counts, they have not consistently demonstrated symptomatic benefit in either direct or indirect comparisons. These findings suggest that although eosinophils play a central role in the pathogenesis and diagnosis of EoE ( 49 , 50 ), they may not be the sole drivers of disease activity. As a T cell-mediated disorder, EoE involves multiple immune pathways and inflammatory mediators beyond eosinophils ( 50 ).

In comparison to agents targeting a single pathway, such as the IL-5 pathway, topical corticosteroids, such as BOS and BOT, exert broader anti-inflammatory effects, targeting multiple cytokine pathways and immune cells. This broader mechanism likely contributes to their observed efficacy across histologic and symptomatic endpoints ( 37 , 38 ), making them first-line therapies for EoE and establishing them as the gold standard for new pharmacological developments. Their use has been associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, including esophageal candidiasis and potential adrenal suppression ( 51 ); however, a recent NMA has shown these risks to be no higher than those observed with placebo or PPls ( 52 ), and adherence may be impacted by the need for twice-daily administration ( 53 ).

Differences in follow-up duration limited direct comparisons of safety outcomes across studies. However, among the included trials that reported safety data, the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events was comparable between biologic agents and placebo, and between steroid agents and placebo ( 7 , 10 , 12 – 15 ). This study has some limitations. Six of the included trials were phase II studies, particularly those comparing mepolizumab 300 mg and ATP-1011 (1.5mg and 3mg), and etrasimod (Tmg and 2mg), with sample sizes ranging from 19 to 41 participants.

Additionally, trials of PPI agents, which are the most commonly prescribed first-line treatment option for EoE ( 54 ), and most swallowed topical corticosteroids (budesonide [aerosolized/swallowed], fluticasone [aerosolized/swallowed], and BOT) had follow-up durations of only 6 to 8 weeks. To reduce heterogeneity, these trials were excluded from the analysis, as no data were available for biologic therapies with follow-up periods of less than 12 weeks. However, this exclusion represents a limitation, particularly given that therapies such as PPIs and swallowed topical corticosteroids are widely used in clinical practice, and excluding these trials may reduce the applicability of our findings.

The limited duration of most corticosteroid trials constrains our ability to assess their utility in the treatment hierarchy of EoE, especially over the long term. We identified three placebo-controlled trials of topical corticosteroids with a 12-week duration for inclusion in our analyses, but only one trial had longer follow-up. Furthermore, as mentioned above, most trials of topical corticosteroids are only 6–8 weeks in duration and therefore not useful for assessing outcomes beyond very short-term effects.

Furthermore, the scarcity of long-term data on biological therapies limits our ability to assess their utility for long-term treatment of EoE. Direct comparisons of biologic agents beyond 24 weeks were not feasible, except for cendakimab.

Our results at 48 weeks, in particular, should be interpreted with caution. First, some trials transitioned patients from placebo to the active comparator arm at 24 weeks (e.g., dupilumab, benralizumab), which prevents assessment of long-term comparative efficacy beyond 24 weeks. Second, only two trials with outcomes at 48 weeks were identified in our review: one with two doses of BOT and placebo and one with two dosing schedules of cendakimab and placebo. Furthermore, BOT was evaluated as maintenance therapy in patients already in histologic remission, whereas cendakimab was assessed in patients with active EoE undergoing induction followed by maintenance. Thus, limited data and differences in trial design necessitate caution when interpreting our findings for outcomes at 48 weeks.

Furthermore, safety data were insufficiently reported across trials, particularly regarding the comparative safety profiles of biologic and corticosteroid therapies, which remain a significant knowledge gap.

In conclusion, this analysis suggests that dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, BOS 2mg, and BOT 0.5 mg and Img are among the most effective agents for improving both dysphagia and endoscopic outcomes in patients with EoE. All evaluated therapies—including biologies and topical corticosteroids—were effective in achieving histologic remission or response. Nonetheless, direct comparative data between biologies and corticosteroids remain limited, particularly regarding long-term efficacy, symptom resolution, and safety. Future head-to-head trials are warranted to evaluate these agents more comprehensively, with a focus on dysphagia-related outcomes, endoscopic improvement, and adverse event profiles to better guide therapeutic decision-making in EoE.

What You Need to Know BACKGROUND Biologic agents and swallowed topical steroids are increasingly used for eosinophilic esophagitis, but comparative, time-specific effects on symptoms, histology, and endoscopy in adolescents and adults remain unclear. FINDINGS Across 13 randomized trials, dupilumab, cendakimab, and oral budesonide provided consistent dysphagia improvement, while most therapies achieved histologic remission, revealing a frequent dissociation between symptom and tissue responses.

IMPLICATIONS FOR PATIENT CARE Clinicians should prioritize therapies with proven symptomatic benefit, recognize that histologic remission may not predict symptom relief, and tailor EoE treatment choices by outcome domain and treatment duration.

Abstract Background Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, food allergen-mediated, esophageal disease that will lead, if left untreated, to esophageal remodeling. As such, the vast majority of EoE patients need treatment. Treatment strategies include drugs, food elimination diets, and esophageal dilation. This review focuses on pharmacologic options for treatment of EoE.

Summary Orodispersible budesonide tablets (Jorveza ® ) have been approved by regulatory authorities for EoE treatment of adults in Europe, Canada, and Australia, but not in the USA. Jorveza ® , as compared to placebo, is effective in inducing and maintaining histologic and clinical remission over time. An orodispersible budesonide suspension (BOS, Eohilia ® ) was recently approved in the USA as induction treatment (12 weeks) in adolescents of at least 11 years and adults with active EoE. Before the approval of Jorveza ® and Eohilia ® , several investigator-initiated randomized controlled clinical studies evaluated esophagus-targeted formulations of either budesonide or fluticasone to treat pediatric and adult EoE patients. These drugs were generally efficacious in inducing and maintaining histological and clinical remission. Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) are used off-label for EoE treatment of pediatric and adult EoE patients given that they are able to induce histologic and clinical remission. However, when compared to the moderate certainty of evidence with regard to the failure to achieve histologic remission with swallowed topical corticosteroids, the certainty of evidence for PPIs is very low with very inconsistent results in absolute terms. Dupilumab (Dupixent ® ), a monoclonal antibody targeted against IL-4 and IL-13, was approved by regulatory authorities in the USA, Europe, Canada, but not yet Australia. In Europe, including Switzerland, Dupixent ® is approved to treat EoE patients of at least 12 years of age with at least 40 kg body weight if they are either unresponsive or intolerant to or not candidates for conventional EoE therapies. Due to lack of efficacy or unfavorable safety profile, the following drugs are not recommended for EoE treatment: systemic steroids, sodium cromoglycate, montelukast, azathioprine, TNF-antagonists (e.g., infliximab), vedolizumab (mAb against α4β7), benralizumab (mAb against IL-5 receptor), mepolizumab (mAb against IL-5), reslizumab (mAb against IL-5), omalizumab (mAb against IgE), and lirentelimab (mAb against Siglec-8).

Key Messages Long-term effectiveness and safety data on different drugs are currently sparse. Concerted efforts of different stakeholders will be necessary to continue the endeavor of providing our patients with much-needed therapies.

EoE is a chronic, local, immune-mediated esophageal disease, characterized, clinically, by symptoms related to esophageal dysfunction and, histologically, by eosinophil-predominant inflammation [ 3 ]. Other systemic and local causes of esophageal eosinophilia should be excluded. Over the last two decades, EoE has transformed from a rare condition to a disease that is commonly encountered with current incidence estimates ranging from 5 to 10 cases per 100,000, and current prevalence estimates ranging from 0.5 to 1 case per 1,000 [ 4 , 5 ]. Concomitant allergies to various food antigens and/or aeroallergens are found in the majority of EoE patients [ 3 ]. In affected children, food refusal, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)-like symptoms, vomiting, and abdominal pain are the leading symptoms, while adolescents and adults mostly present with dysphagia for solids and/or food impaction [ 3 , 6 ]. Adult EoE patients frequently adapt to living with dysphagia by practicing various behaviors, such as food avoidance, food modification, or they take a longer time for ingestion of certain foods compared to other people eating that same food [ 7 ]. Histologic diagnosis is based on the presence of ≥15 esophageal eosinophils/high-power field (hpf) and exclusion of other diagnoses potentially associated with esophageal eosinophilia [ 3 ]. In the vast majority of patients, untreated, eosinophil-predominant inflammation leads to formation of strictures that are associated with the occurrence of food bolus impactions, which carry the inherent risk of esophageal perforations [ 5 , 8 ]. In fact, once anti-eosinophil treatments are stopped, histologic or clinical relapse rates exceed 90% over a 1-year period [ 9 ]. Treatment options range from pharmacologic and diet therapies to esophageal dilation [ 10 – 12 ]. The optimal long-term therapeutic approach still needs to be defined. EoE activity is assessed using a combination of patient-reported outcomes (PROs; encompasses EoE-related symptoms and quality of life) as well as histologic and endoscopic activity [ 13 ]. In randomized placebo-controlled trials, EoE-related symptoms are measured using an electronic daily diary, such as the Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ) or the symptom-based Eosinophilic Esophagitis Activity Index (EEsAI) PROs (recall period of 7 days), while histologic activity is assessed using the Eosinophilic Esophagitis Histologic Scoring System (EoE-HSS) that describes the grade and stage of eight distinct histologic features [ 14 ]. Endoscopic activity should be assessed using the Endoscopic Reference Score (EREFS) [ 14 ]. This review focuses on pharmacologic treatment options for EoE and will discuss neither food elimination diets nor esophageal dilation. In clinical practice, the therapy choice is strongly dependent on, among others, the EoE phenotype (purely inflammatory features vs. fibrotic features or a combination of both), presence of atopic comorbidities requiring treatment, the patient-perceived impact of the disease, and patient preferences.

Swallowed Topical Corticosteroids (Budesonide, Fluticasone, Ciclesonide) This section highlights the use of swallowed topical corticosteroids as induction and maintenance treatment. Safety aspects are also discussed.

Swallowed topical corticosteroids are efficacious in inducing histologic and clinical remission in pediatric and adult EoE patients. A meta-analysis of 7 studies with 250 participants found that symptomatic improvement was more frequently achieved in patients taking swallowed topical corticosteroids when compared to the control group (placebo or PPIs) (OR: 3.03, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.57–5.87) [ 18 ]. Histological remission was more frequently achieved in patients taking swallowed topical corticosteroids when compared to control groups (placebo or PPIs; 330 participants, OR: 13.66, 95% CI: 2.65–70.34) [ 18 ]. It should be noted that the comparison of results among different studies is limited by the variability in used agents (budesonide, fluticasone, ciclesonide), delivery systems (suspension, viscous slurry, swallowed puffs from inhalers, effervescent tablets), dosing, treatment periods, and the definition of histologic remission (ranges from <1 up to <20 eosinophils/hpf) and clinical remission (use of several, sometimes unvalidated PRO instruments) [ 13 ]. A comparative analysis of different dosages used in the various studies has been carried out in the recently published British EoE guidelines [ 49 ]. Dellon et al. [ 19 ] showed that, during an 8-week treatment duration, viscous topical budesonide (1 mg twice daily) was more effective than nebulized (and then swallowed) budesonide to reduce peak eosinophil counts per hpf (11 vs. 89, p = 0.02). In addition, authors showed that the medication contact time with the mucosa, as measured by scintigraphy, was higher for the group being treated with oral viscous budesonide (OVB) when compared to the group treated with nebulized budesonide ( p < 0.005) [ 19 ]. In a double-blind, double-dummy trial lasting 8 weeks, OVB administered at the dose of 1 mg twice daily was equivalent to fluticasone multidose inhaler (MDI) administered at the dose of 880 μg twice daily in inducing histologic (71% OVB vs. 64% MDI, p = 0.38) and clinical response (posttreatment DSQ scores were 5 and 4 in the OVB and MDI groups, p = 0.70) [ 20 ]. Similar trends were noted for posttreatment total EREFS (2 vs. 3; p = 0.06) [ 20 ]. Esophageal candidiasis developed in 12% of patients receiving OVB and 16% of patients receiving MDI; oral thrush was observed in 3% and 2%, respectively [ 20 ]. One trial with 4 children evaluated ciclesonide, a topical glucocorticoid with less systemic absorption than fluticasone, and showed that symptoms as well as eosinophil counts decreased after 2 months of treatment [ 21 ]. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial to assess the effectiveness and tolerability of a budesonide orodispersible tablet (BOT, 1 mg twice daily; n = 59) or placebo ( n = 29) showed that at 6 weeks, 58% of patients given BOT were in combined clinical and histologic remission compared with 0 patients given placebo ( p < 0.0001) [ 15 ]. At week 6, histologic remission was achieved by 93% of patients given BOT versus no patients under placebo ( p < 0.0001). After 12 weeks, 85% of patients had achieved combined clinical and histological remission [ 15 ]. Six-week BOT administration and 12-week BOT administration were safe and well tolerated; 5% of patients who received BOT developed symptomatic, mild candida, which was easily treated with an oral antifungal agent [ 15 ]. Based on these results, in November 2017, budesonide in a form of a melting tablet (Jorveza ® ) was the first esophagus-specific formulation to be granted approval by the European Medicines Agency as induction treatment for adults with EoE, benefitting from an orphan drug designation [ 50 ]. Jorveza ® is currently also available in Great Britain, Canada, and Australia.

The Food and Drug Administration approved in February 2024 EOHILIA ® 2 mg twice daily, an oral budesonide suspension (BOS, 2 mg/10 mL single-dose stick packs), based on efficacy and safety data from two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled 12-week studies in patients aged 11 to 55 years [ 16 , 51 ]. In both studies, patients received at least one dose of either BOS 2 mg twice daily or placebo orally twice daily. Efficacy endpoints included histologic remission (peak eosinophil count of ≤6/hpf) and the absolute change from baseline in DSQ combined score after 12 weeks of treatment. Significantly more patients receiving BOS achieved histologic remission versus placebo in study 1 (53.1% vs. 1%). In study 2, 38% of BOS-treated patients achieved histologic remission versus 2.4% of those in the placebo group. Absolute change from baseline in DSQ combined score in the BOS versus placebo groups in study 1 was −10.2 (1.5) versus −6.5 (1.8) and in study 2, −14.5 (1.8) versus −5.9 (2.1). Of note, BOS (EOHILIA ® ) is only approved as induction treatment for 12 weeks, not as maintenance treatment.

EoE is a chronic progressive disorder with a high recurrence rate in the absence of anti-eosinophil treatment [ 22 ]. As such, the vast majority of patients need a long-term maintenance treatment. There is a paucity of studies evaluating the long-term efficacy (LTE) of swallowed topical steroids in pediatric and adult EoE patients. In a 50-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Straumann et al. [ 23 ] evaluated the efficacy of swallowed topical budesonide suspension given at the dose of 0.5 mg/day versus placebo. Histologic remission, defined as <5 eosinophils/hpf, was found in 36% of patients in the budesonide group, while no patient in the placebo group remained in remission [ 23 ]. One important learning point from this landmark study was that the daily dosage of budesonide was too low to maintain EoE in histologic remission in the majority of patients. An open-label, prospective, single-center study in children examined age-dependent dosages of swallowed topical fluticasone from a metered dose inhaler. Patients enrolled in the study showed an improvement with respect to histology, endoscopy, and symptoms over a mean follow-up time of 24 months [ 24 ]. A recently published double-blind trial by Straumann et al. [ 9 ] compared the efficacy and safety of 2 dosages of BOT versus placebo in maintaining remission defined as absence of clinical and histologic relapse and no premature withdrawal for any reason in adults with EoE. Two hundred and four adults with EoE in clinical and histologic remission were randomly assigned to groups given BOT 0.5 mg twice daily ( n = 68), BOT 1.0 mg twice daily ( n = 68), or placebo twice daily ( n = 68) for up to 48 weeks. After 48 weeks, 73.5% of patients receiving BOT 0.5 mg twice daily and 75% receiving BOT 1.0 mg twice daily were in persistent remission compared with 4.4% of patients in the placebo group ( p < 0.001 for both comparisons of BOT with placebo) [ 9 ]. Median time to relapse in the placebo group was 87 days. This landmark study paved the way for the approval of BOT (Jorveza ® ) as a maintenance therapy.

With respect to safety aspects, the use of swallowed topical corticosteroids in the short term and long term seems to be characterized by a favorable safety profile with no serious side effects. In the BOT (Jorveza ® ) maintenance trial over 48 weeks, the frequency of adverse events was similar in the BOT and placebo groups. Of note, morning serum levels of cortisol were in the normal range at baseline and did not significantly change during treatment. Four patients receiving BOT developed asymptomatic, low serum levels of cortisol. Clinically manifested candidiasis was suspected in 16.2% of patients in the BOT 0.5 mg group and in 11.8% of patients in the BOT 1.0 mg group; all infections resolved with treatment. There are conflicting results regarding the long-term use of swallowed topical steroids and their impact on adrenal suppression, particularly in children. Philla et al. [ 52 ] observed no differences in serum cortisol levels in 14 children treated with either swallowed fluticasone propionate (range 220–880 µg/day) or budesonide (range 0.5–1 mg/day) for a duration of 8–43 weeks. However, Golekoh et al. [ 53 ] documented adrenal suppression in 10% of children ( n = 58) treated with swallowed topical steroids for ≥6 months. No symptoms of adrenal insufficiency or impaired growth were reported so far. Inhaled topical steroids for asthma treatment are associated with an increased risk for osteoporosis [ 54 ]. Such an association has not yet been described for swallowed topical corticosteroids in EoE.

In conclusion, swallowed topical steroids appear to be efficacious/effective in inducing clinical and histologic remission in pediatric and adult EoE patients. This class of medications appears to have a favorable safety profile. The oral budesonide tablet (BOT, Jorveza ® ) has been approved for induction and maintenance treatment of adults with EoE in several countries outside the USA, while the oral budesonide suspension (BOS, EOHILIA ® ) has been approved as induction treatment only for adolescents and adults with EoE in the USA. Given that no swallowed topical corticosteroid-based product has been approved yet for treatment of pediatric EoE patients under age of 11 years, several extemporaneous preparations of swallowed topical corticosteroids will continue to be used in this population. Long-term follow-up of EoE patients in prospective cohort studies will be best suited to systematically document long-term side effects associated with this class of medication [ 55 ].

Proton-Pump Inhibitors GERD may mimic, coexist with, or exacerbate EoE [ 56 ]. On the other hand, EoE can also contribute to GERD activity by impacting esophageal clearance [ 57 ]. EoE patients may profit from PPI therapy, as it reduces acid production in patients with coexistent GERD and inhibits homing of eosinophils to the esophageal mucosa [ 58 ]. PPIs may also be used in patients with established EoE, as the altered esophagus may be more sensitive to physiologic acid exposure [ 59 ]. While in mechanistic terms PPIs may be useful as single or add-on therapy, it is important to remember that as of today no placebo-controlled trial has been conducted to evaluate PPI efficacy in EoE.

A recently published systematic review and meta-analysis, guided by the AGA Institute and the Joint Task Force on Allergy-Immunology Practice Parameters, evaluated the efficacy of PPIs for the endpoint “not achieving histologic remission” (defined as <15 eosinophils/hpf) for a treatment duration of 8 weeks in 23 studies with a total of 1,051 participants [ 25 ]. Authors found that 58.3% (unweighted) of subjects on PPIs failed to achieve histopathologic remission compared to 86.7% (unweighted) of a placebo control group [ 58 ]. As such, the relative effect of PPIs for not achieving histologic remission was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.61–0.72). When assessing the quality of evidence, the certainty in the effect estimate was considered to be very low and the certainty in the estimate was downgraded given very inconsistent results in absolute terms [ 25 ]. Of note, the authors did not evaluate the relative effect of PPIs on symptom improvement in EoE [ 25 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2016 that included 33 studies with 619 patients showed that PPIs led to histological remission (defined as <15 eosinophils/hpf) in 50.5% (95% CI 42.2–58.7%) and symptomatic improvement in 60.8% (95% CI 48.4–72.2%) of patients [ 26 ]. The authors detected no significant differences in patients’ age, study design, and type of PPIs used [ 26 ]. They observed a trend for increased clinical and histologic efficacy when PPIs were given twice daily when compared to an administration once daily and also in patients with a pathological pH monitoring [ 26 ]. Furthermore, the authors provided a word of caution regarding the interpretation of their findings due to poor-quality evidence, heterogeneity in results, and publication bias in favor of studies reporting histological responses to PPIs. PPIs may also be effective in maintaining clinical and histologic remission. A prospective study in a pediatric cohort showed that most patients (78%) remained in clinico-pathologic remission at the 1-year follow-up on maintenance PPI therapy [ 27 ]. The first long-term follow-up multicenter study in 75 adult patients revealed that all patients who temporarily discontinued PPI therapy had a symptomatic and/or histologic relapse [ 28 ]. A total of 73% of patients maintained histological remission after at least 1 year when PPI dosages were tapered to the minimum effective clinical dose. Most patients who relapsed regained histological remission after dose escalation, which suggests that some patients might require high-dose PPI therapy in the long-term run [ 28 ]. PPIs are prescribed off-label for treatment of pediatric and adult EoE patients. It is very unlikely that PPIs will be granted official approval by regulatory authorities in the near future given the low interest of pharmaceutical companies to invest in clinical trials in EoE.

Systemic Steroids Systemic steroids are not recommended for use in EoE given their side-effect profile and the generally high efficacy of topical swallowed steroids [ 3 , 49 ]. One randomized trial evaluated oral prednisone ( n = 40) versus swallowed topical fluticasone ( n = 40) in pediatric EoE patients [ 31 ]. At week four, almost all patients, irrespective of the treatment group, were free of symptoms, whereas histologic improvement was noted to be greater in the prednisone group. As expected, glucocorticoid side effects were more frequently observed in the prednisone group when compared to the fluticasone group [ 31 ].

Azathioprine, Mercaptopurine One case series with 3 patients documented a clinical and histologic response on azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine in EoE patients dependent on prednisone [ 32 ]. One factor limiting the use of these drugs is their side-effect profile [ 33 ].

Anti-Allergic Drugs: Sodium Cromoglycate, Leukotriene, and Prostaglandin Receptor Antagonists Several anti-allergic drugs were evaluated for EoE treatment but failed to show a clinically relevant benefit regarding histologic activity or EoE-related symptoms. A 4-week trial of the mast cell stabilizer sodium cromoglycate failed to show either symptomatic or histologic improvement in 14 children with EoE [ 34 ]. Montelukast is a leukotriene D4 receptor antagonist. In open-label trials, montelukast use in high doses in adults and standard doses in children led to a symptomatic improvement but failed to demonstrate a histologic response [ 35 , 36 ]. In a randomized controlled trial, Alexander and coworkers found that montelukast (20 mg per day) was not superior to placebo in maintaining remission induced by swallowed topical steroids [ 37 ]. Similarly, montelukast failed to maintain remission induced by swallowed topical steroids in a prospective study in adult EoE patients with reappearance of symptoms and histologic inflammation within a period of 3 months [ 38 ].

One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluated the efficacy of the oral prostaglandin D2 receptor antagonist OC000459 [ 60 ]. A total of 26 adult patients with steroid-dependent or steroid-refractory EoE were randomized to either receive OC000459 or placebo. At week 8, OC000459 but not placebo was associated with a significant reduction in esophageal eosinophil counts and an improvement in symptoms; however, no normalization of esophageal biopsies was documented [ 60 ]. Biologic Drugs

Dupilumab (Dupixent ® ), a monoclonal antibody targeted against IL-4 and IL-13, was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in May 2022 for treatment of adolescent (≥12 years) and adult patients with EoE. Dupilumab is also approved by regulatory authorities in Europe and Canada. In Europe, including Switzerland, Dupixent ® is approved for treatment of EoE patients of at least 12 years of age with at least 40 kg body weight if these patients are either unresponsive or intolerant to or not candidates for conventional EoE therapies. The approval was based on the positive results of a three-part, phase 3 trial, in which patients 12 years of age or older underwent randomization in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous dupilumab at a weekly dose of 300 mg or placebo (part A) or in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive 300 mg of dupilumab either weekly or every 2 weeks or weekly placebo (part B) up to week 24 [ 17 ]. Eligible patients who completed part A or part B continued the trial in part C. The two primary endpoints at week 24 were histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils per hpf) and the change from baseline in the DSQ score. In part A, histologic remission occurred in 25 of 42 patients (60%) who received weekly dupilumab and in 2 of 39 patients (5%) who received placebo (difference, 55 percentage points; 95% CI: 40–71; p < 0.001). In part B, histologic remission occurred in 47 of 80 patients (59%) with weekly dupilumab, in 49 of 81 patients (60%) with dupilumab every 2 weeks, and in 5 of 79 patients (6%) with placebo (difference between weekly dupilumab and placebo, 54 percentage points; 95% CI: 41–66 [ p < 0.001]; difference between dupilumab every 2 weeks and placebo, 56 percentage points; 95% CI: 43–69 [not significant per hierarchical testing]). The mean (±SD) DSQ scores at baseline were 33.6 ± 12.41 in part A and 36.7 ± 11.22 in part B; the scores improved with weekly dupilumab as compared with placebo, with differences of −12.32 (95% CI: −19.11 to −5.54) in part A and −9.92 (95% CI: −14.81 to −5.02) in part B (both p < 0.001) but not with dupilumab every 2 weeks (difference in part B, −0.51; 95% CI: −5.42 to 4.41). There was a favorable side-effect profile in patients under dupilumab. Given that dupilumab is also approved by European and the US regulators for treatment of moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, moderate-to-severe asthma, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, this medication may be particularly useful in EoE patients with these atopic comorbidities requiring treatment.

Cendakimab is a monoclonal antibody against IL-13. In a placebo-controlled double-blind phase II trial during 16 weeks in 99 patients, cendakimab 360 mg sc once weekly showed significant reductions of peak eosinophil counts, endoscopic severity, and EoE-related symptoms (measured by the dysphagia symptom diary, DSD) as compared to placebo-treated patients [ 29 ]. Cendakimab showed a favorable safety profile. The most common adverse events were headache and upper respiratory tract infection. The LTE and safety of cendakimab were evaluated in the open-label extension study in 66 patients who completed the 16-week induction portion of the abovementioned phase 2 study [ 30 ]. Patients received 360 mg cendakimab sc once a week for 52 weeks. By week 12 of the LTE, esophageal eosinophil mean and peak counts, total EREFS, and EoE-HSS grade and stage scores did not differ considerably between patients who originally received placebo versus cendakimab. Most patients maintained responses through week 52. The rates of patients in symptomatic remission as measured by the EEsAI PRO instrument (score ≤20) increased from 14% at LTE entry to 67% at LTE week 52 in placebo-treated patients switched to cendakimab and from 30% at LTE entry to 54% at LTE week 52 in patients treated with cendakimab during both double-blind and open-label extension phases of the program [ 7 ]. Of the 28 patients who did not have a histologic response to cendakimab during the double-blind induction phase, 10 patients (36%) achieved response during the LTE. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (21%) and nasopharyngitis (14%). A large phase III study evaluating cendakimab has completed recruitment, and first results are to be expected in 2024.

Mepolizumab and reslizumab are both anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibodies that have been evaluated nearly a decade ago in three randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in children, adolescents, and adults with EoE [ 39 – 41 ]. All three trials showed a significant reduction of esophageal eosinophilic infiltrations; however, histologic remission was not observed. An improvement in EoE-related symptoms was found in two studies [ 40 , 41 ].

Benralizumab is a monoclonal antibody against the IL-5 receptor. The drug is already on the market for severe eosinophilic asthma that is insufficiently controlled using standard therapy. Benralizumab is capable of killing eosinophils via a dual mechanism: the blockade of IL-5-mediated survival of these cells and the enhancement of eosinophil apoptosis induced by activation of the FcγRIIIa receptor of NK cells. The double-blind placebo-controlled MESSINA trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of benralizumab in adolescent and adult patients with active EoE and assessed at week 24 the proportion of patients with a histologic response, defined as a peak esophageal eosinophil count ≤6/hpf, and mean changes from baseline in DSQ [ 42 ]. According to a press release from AstraZeneca end of 2022, the endpoint of histologic remission at week 24 was achieved, but there was no difference in DSQ when compared to placebo. The study results are not yet published in a form of a peer-reviewed paper. The results of this study indicate that drugs that selectively deplete eosinophils are not sufficient to improve EoE-related symptoms, as other cells of the Th2 cascade likely play a role in promoting and maintaining inflammation of the esophagus [ 61 ]. Drugs, such as dupilumab or cendakimab, with a more upstream mechanism of action, are likely better suited to treat EoE.

Sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin 8 (Siglec-8) is an inhibitory receptor expressed on eosinophils and mast cells. Lirentelimab is a humanized, anti-Siglec-8 monoclonal antibody that is capable of depleting tissue and blood eosinophils [ 44 ]. Lirentelimab has proven efficacy in Th2 diseases, such as conjunctivitis ( NCT03379311 ) and urticaria ( NCT03436797 ). Lirentelimab was the first biologic to be investigated for its efficacy in a randomized placebo-controlled trial in 65 adults with eosinophilic gastritis or eosinophilic duodenitis [ 45 ]. Assessment of eosinophil counts in the gastric and duodenal tissues was performed before and following 12-week treatment; assessment of esophageal eosinophilia was carried out in those patients, who had a prior diagnosis of EoE. Mean decrease in gastric/duodenal eosinophils was 86% in lirentelimab-treated patients compared to 9% in placebo [ 45 ]. Total symptom score decreased by 48% in the lirentelimab arm and only by 22% in the placebo arm. Sustained tissue eosinophil suppression was seen in patients participating in the open-label extension part of the study. Twenty patients with concomitant esophageal eosinophilia were analyzed in this study. Of the 14 patients treated with lirentelimab, 13 patients demonstrated resolution of esophageal eosinophilia. Of the 9 patients treated with placebo, only 1 patient reached that outcome. Although reduction in symptoms following treatment with lirentelimab was observed, complete symptom response was not reported. Lirentelimab was further evaluated in the phase III KRYPTOS study ( clinicaltrials.gov NCT04322708 ) [ 46 ]. Group 1 ( n = 93) was treated with a monthly injection of 1 mg/kg of lirentelimab for 6 months, group 2 ( n = 91) received a monthly injection of 3 mg/kg of lirentelimab, and group 3 ( n = 92) was treated with placebo. After 24 weeks, a histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils/hpf) was achieved in 92.5% (group 1), 87.9% (group 2), and 10.9% (placebo), respectively. However, change in DSQ was not different in lirentelimab-treated patients when compared to placebo. This trial shows that selective depletion of eosinophils and mast cells is not sufficient to provide symptomatic improvement. In addition, this study questions the utility of assessing eosinophil counts alone as an endpoint in randomized controlled clinical trials in EoE. Results of the KRYPTOS study have not been published yet as a peer-reviewed paper.

Omalizumab is a monoclonal anti-IgE antibody. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adult EoE patients showed no benefits of omalizumab over placebo with respect to improvement in esophageal eosinophil counts and EoE-related symptoms [ 43 ]. Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against tumor necrosis factor. Infliximab at a dosage of 5 mg/kg body weight was evaluated in 3 adult EoE patients. An induction treatment at weeks 0, 2, and 6 did not lead to an improvement of EoE-related symptoms and esophageal eosinophilia [ 47 ]. Other monoclonal antibodies against tumor necrosis factor, such as adalimumab or golimumab, have not been evaluated in EoE patients.

Vedolizumab is a monoclonal antibody against α4β7 that is expressed on T-lymphocytes and also eosinophils. Blockade of α4β7 inhibits the interaction with MAdCAM-1 expressed by endothelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract. The drug is marketed for treatment of patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. One case report of a patient suffering from Crohn’s disease and concomitant EoE described resolution of EoE, when the patient was switched from infliximab to vedolizumab [ 48 ].

Comparative Effectiveness of Different Drugs in EoE A recently published systematic review and meta-analysis in 15 studies containing 1,813 patients evaluated the efficacy of the following drugs to induce histologic remission as well as clinical and endoscopic response: lirentelimab, budesonide orodispersible tablet (BOT, Jorveza ® ), benralizumab, fluticasone orodispersible tablet, dupilumab (Dupixent ® ), esomeprazole, budesonide oral suspension (BOS), fluticasone (aerosolized and then swallowed), cendakimab, mepolizumab, and budesonide (aerosolized and then swallowed) [ 62 ]. For histological remission defined as ≤15 eosinophils/HPF, BOT 1 mg two times per day ranked first. For failure to achieve symptom improvement, BOT 1 mg two times per day and budesonide oral suspension (BOS) 2 mg two times per day were significantly more efficacious than placebo. For failure to achieve endoscopic improvement based on the EoE EREFS, BOT 1 mg two times per day and BOS 1 mg two times per day or 2 mg two times per day were significantly more efficacious than placebo. The authors also mention that an important heterogeneity in eligibility criteria and outcome measures among available trials hampers the establishment of a solid therapeutic hierarchy.

Conclusions Despite the fact that the first EoE patients have been described only 30 years ago, considerable progress has been made in evaluating different treatment options as well as in understanding the pathophysiology and the natural history of this condition. Therapeutic options in EoE include drugs, elimination diets, and esophageal dilation. Orodispersible budesonide tablets (Jorveza ® ) have been approved by regulatory authorities for EoE treatment of adults in Europe, Canada, and Australia, but not in the USA. Jorveza ® is efficacious in inducing and maintaining histologic and clinical remission compared to placebo. An orodispersible budesonide suspension (BOS, Eohilia ® ) was approved in February 2024 as induction treatment for adolescents of at least 11 years and adults with EoE in the USA only. Before the approval of Jorveza ® and Eohilia ® , several investigator-initiated clinical studies evaluated esophagus-targeted formulations of either budesonide or fluticasone to treat pediatric and adult EoE patients. These studies have generally shown that these medications are effective in inducing histological and clinical remission. Given the fact that PPIs are able to induce histologic and clinical remission albeit with very low quality of evidence and very inconsistent results of mostly observational studies, this class of medications is used off-label for EoE treatment of both pediatric and adult EoE patients. Dupilumab (Dupixent ® ), a monoclonal antibody against IL-4 and IL-13, was approved by regulatory authorities in the USA, Europe, and Canada. Cendakimab (mAb against IL-13) is a promising candidate for EoE treatment; results of a phase III trial are expected in 2024. Due to lack of efficacy or unfavorable safety profile, the following drugs are not recommended for EoE treatment: systemic steroids, sodium cromoglycate, montelukast, azathioprine, infliximab, vedolizumab (mAb against α4β7), benralizumab (mAb against IL-5 receptor), mepolizumab (mAb against IL-5), reslizumab (mAb against IL-5), omalizumab (mAb against IgE), and lirentelimab (mAb against Siglec-8). LTE/effectiveness and safety data with the different drugs are currently sparse. Concerted efforts of different stakeholders will be necessary to continue the endeavor of providing our patients with much-needed therapies.

For commercial re-use, please contact journals.permissions@oup.com Summary Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic immune-mediated disease requiring a long-term maintenance treatment. The data on therapy patterns and treatment durability in the biologic era are scarce in a real-world setting. The aim of this project was to provide information on the treatment courses in a real-world setting over past 10 years. Data on demographics, concomitant atopic diseases and treatments were collected retrospectively at seven Austrian centres. The eligible subjects had to start their first therapy between January 2014 and February 2025. In total, 336 patients (30.1% female) were analyzed of whom 34.5% remained on the first line treatment. In a mean time of 7.6 months, a second line treatment was started. The most common first line treatment was swallowed topical corticosteroids (STCs) (54.2%), followed by proton pump inhibitors (22.3%) and food elimination diet (6.0%). In contrast to only a minority who continued on PPI therapy after starting it (21.3%), the majority of patients had ongoing STC treatment (51%). Forty-one (12.2%) patients received a treatment with dupilumab of whom only one as first line treatment (because of multiple type 2 inflammatory diseases) and the majority as second line treatment (57.5%). The reasons for dupilumab were non-response to STC (59%), followed by side effects (24%). 97.6% (40/41) of them remained on dupilumab until the last follow-up. Although most patients receive STC at the beginning, the majority need multiple treatment lines. However, until 2018 there was no approved medication to treat EoE. Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) 2 and off-label swallowed topical corticosteroids (olSTC) were the most used medications in European countries. After approval of the budesonide orodispersible tablet (BOT) in the European Union (EU), BOT is, at least in German speaking countries, the most recommended medication for first line treatment. 3 Furthermore, STC are recommended by the American Gastroenterology Association (AGA) with a ‘strong’ strength of recommendation as opposed to PPI that have only a ‘conditional’ strength of recommendation to treat EoE. 4 However, PPIs, STC, and dietary elimination are all considered as valid first line treatment options in EoE. The approval of dupilumab, an IL-4R antagonist, as the first biologic expanded the armamentarium to treat EoE and challenged the existing equality of first-line medications. Currently, due to costs and availability, dupilumab is used as second or even as third line therapy after STC and PPI. However, in patients with other type 2 inflammatory diseases such as asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with polyposis nasi or atopic dermatitis, dupilumab may be used as first line treatment in order to avoid steroid effects from different topical usages. There exists rarely any real-world study investigating multiple therapeutic lines in the era of biologics. 5

We collected real-world data from seven Austrian centers on long-term management of EoE patients and their therapy courses in order to close this knowledge gap. We assessed different therapy lines throughout the years and investigated specifically the indication of dupilumab and the course of disease in these patients. Furthermore, we evaluated the time on each treatment line and the most common reasons for change and/or discontinuation.

METHODS We conducted a nation-wide retrospective study involving seven centers in Austria. Patients with EoE who received the first-line therapy between January 2014 and February 2025 were included. Data on demographic, previous medical history and therapy courses were collected from the electronic health data records.

For each established treatment line, the type of medication, duration and reason for change or discontinuation were evaluated. Previously, the treatment was commonly discontinued after induction of the short-term remission as there were no sufficient data on the long-term efficacy. 6 In case of a relapse, if the same drug that induced remission was re-established, this was still considered as the same therapy line. Information on dosing and dosing interval was not obtained. Food elimination diets (FED) were differentiated based on the number of products excluded. Subjects could receive several therapeutic approaches at once. Only patients that received any form of the therapy (either dietary or pharmaceutical intervention) were included. The date of the last endoscopy within the follow-up period and the number of eosinophils/high power field at that timepoint were recorded as well. Neither patients’ reported outcomes nor endoscopic scores were available from the timepoints of the therapy change.

Dichotomous variables are presented as fractions, the continuous variables as means with standard deviation (SD). No power analysis for sample size estimation was performed. For association testing between categorical variables, Chi-square test was used. To test the association between diagnostic delay and probability to remain on BOT, a new ordinal variable was introduced (diagnostic delay <2 years, 2–5 years, 5–10 years, > 10 years) and then Chi-square test was performed. Missing data were not imputed. All statistical analyses were carried out in R v.4.2.1. (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria). Flow diagrams were created with SankeyMatic v.1.2.0. The figures were created with R v.4.2.1. (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria) and BioRender (Toronto, Canada).

The project was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical University of Vienna (1783/2024). The study was performed in accordance with Declaration of Helsinki 1964. Diagnostic delay (time from the symptoms onset to a histologic diagnosis) was 6.8 years (± 8.9 years, Table 1 ). Mean follow-up time was 4.9 years (± 3.9 years). BOT as first-line therapy For clarity purposes, we present the data for those who received a combination therapy separately ( Supplementary Table 1 ). 51.1% of BOT only patients (93/182) were still on the drug at the timepoint of the data collection. On the other hand, the mean discontinuation time was 7.0 months (± 10.9 months). The most common reason for the discontinuation was achievement of clinical or histologic remission (24 out of 89 subjects who discontinued, 27.0%), followed by side effects (15.7%). Fifty-nine patients in this group received a second-line therapy ( Fig. 3 ) with PPI (22/59, 37.3%) or dupilumab (22/59, 37.3%) as the two most common second line therapies. Figure 3 summarizes the treatment courses of this subgroup in a schematic way. One patient received tezepelumab as off-label treatment. At the time of the last follow-up, 32 patients did not receive any therapy or there were no available data on the current treatment. We observed no association between age at inclusion, diagnostic delay, concomitant atopic diseases, sex and previous bolus impaction and the probability to remain on BOT as first line therapy.

In all but one cases this was dupilumab. One person was treated with an off-label treatment with tezepelumab, a monoclonal antibody against thymic stromal lymphopoietin. 7 Since tezepelumab is a not approved medication, we analysed only 41 patients. Mean age at inclusion was 40.9 years, 41.5% were female and the majority had another type 2 inflammatory disease (53.7%) ( Table 2 ). Twenty-four patients (24/41, 58.5%) received dupilumab as a second line therapy due to non-response or loss of response to the previous therapy, followed by side effects of the previous therapy ( Fig. 6 ). At the time of the last follow-up, the mean time on the drug was 8.0 months (± 5.4 months). There was only one discontinuation of dupilumab. We were able to obtain histological data from the last endoscopy after the beginning of the biologic treatment for 25 individuals (25/41, 61.0%). The mean eosinophilic count per high-power field was 5.8 (SD: 17.4). Seventeen patients had histologic remission (0 eosinophils per high-power field; 17/25, 68.0%).
