DISCUSSION Although the therapeutic armamentarium in EoE is growing, an established therapeutic pyramid, similar to inflammatory bowel diseases, is lacking. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-world study on therapy courses in the biologic era in patients with EoE.

Our retrospective real-world analysis of 336 EoE patients demonstrates following findings: (i) Although BOT are used in most cases as first-line therapy, only half of patients continued this treatment option during follow-up; (ii) Nearly 80% of patients starting with a PPI changed the therapy during follow-up, mostly due to non/loss-of response; (iii) A tenth of patients received dupilumab, mostly as a second-line therapy due to non/loss-of response of the previous therapy; and (iv) Although 62.2% of the patients needed one or two treatment lines, around 10% had multiple treatment lines due to loss-of response or side-effects.

Since EoE is a chronic immune-mediated disease with a progressive nature from an inflammatory to a fibrostenotic disease in many patients, long-term treatment is nearly always necessary. In line with the newest guideline from the American College of Gastroenterology strongly recommending STC in contrast to PPI and empiric FED as therapy for EoE, 8 the majority of our patients started the approved BOT as first line treatment. Our data also confirm a recently published study that BOT is the preferred first-line drug of Austrian providers. 3 Since robust maintenance data of BOT showed a high clinical and histologic remission rate without any new safety signal up to 3 years, 9 there exist no reasonable reason to change or stop BOT after inducing remission. If we consider the 20% of patients that stopped BOT due to response to therapy, the number of patients on maintenance with BOT are similar to other real-life data. 10 Admittedly, it remains unclear whether patients stopped their therapy on their own or due to recommendation of the treating physician. Although we cannot pinpoint the exact reason for stopping the medication, the lack of understanding about the chronicity of EoE 11 and fear of side effects 12 play probably a significant role.

In contrast to the preferred first-line therapy in Spain and Italy, only a minority of the patients in our study started a therapy with PPI. 5 However, our data are similar to the data from Switzerland 13 , 14 in which most patients are treated with STC and only a small number is treated with PPI. More interesting, however, is the fact that only a small number of patients continued treatment with the PPI over the course of the study and the majority changed medication due to treatment failure. The effectiveness of PPIs in our data is worse than in a recently published meta-analysis of 73 studies 15 and of the real-world analysis from Spain and Italy. 5 However, as we were unable to determine the exact dosage of used PPI in our data, one possible explanation is that the dose in our population was too low, which led to a poorer histologic or symptomatic response.

Although diet is the only therapeutic option that gets to the root of the problem and despite the fact that data confirm the effectiveness of FED in EoE, 16 even as long-term management at least in a US population, 17 several cohort studies show that only a small fraction of patients choose and follow this therapeutic option. 5 , 14 Compared to the Swiss cohort and the EoE CONNECT database, a similar number of our patients started a FED, half of them with a 1-FED. However, most patients switched or added a medication in the course of disease due to non-response or feasibility. These results are not surprising, as FED is judged by patients as the most inconvenient therapy, at least in Switzerland. 18 However, despite the hurdles and challenges of changing a diet, in the US, many EoE patients prefer to follow a FED over a long-term medication. 11 Hence, we can suppose that Austrian patients have a similar cultural background as the Swiss neighbors and therefore are reluctant to follow a diet that excludes dietary products.

Recently, dupilumab—an IL-4Rα antagonist—has emerged as another effective treatment option for EoE 19 and is approved as the first and nowadays only biologic in Europe since 2023. So far, only two real-world studies from the US showed the efficacy of dupilumab in 70 and 46 patients, respectively. 20 , 21 However, since BOT is available in Europe as another approved medication to treat EoE and the reimbursement policy is different compared to the US, these two studies are difficult to compare with our data, especially with regard to the indication of dupilumab.

More than 10% of patients switched, mostly because of non-response or loss of response to a previous therapy, to dupilumab over the disease course. Interestingly, 24.4% switched to dupilumab due to side effects from previous therapies and one patient started dupilumab as first-line therapy due to other type 2 inflammatory diseases. However, although these patients may need multiple topical corticosteroids resulting in a high cumulative steroid burden, 22 it has to be kept in mind that cost-effectiveness of dupilumab is currently suboptimal as first-line treatment, at least shown in a Markov model in the US. 23 Nearly all patients that switched to dupilumab remained on this therapy until the end of follow-up and were in histological remission at the last endoscopy.

Our study is not without limitations. Due to its retrospective design, some endoscopic data was missing and the reason for switching the medication was not always traceable. However, most data came from patients who started therapy in the last 3 years and who are still being treated in the respective centers. Another limitation is the small number of patients that started a FED making any conclusion about effectivity of diet difficult.

In conclusion, this real-world analysis of more than 300 patients with EoE demonstrates that most patients use BOT as first-line therapy and half of them continue this medication for several years. Most patients starting a PPI will eventually switch to another therapeutic option and finally, more than 10% of patients will need a therapy with dupilumab. BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, inflammatory disease of the esophagus with a rapidly increasing incidence. However, population-based epidemiologic data on EoE are rare and limited to regions with less than 200,000 inhabitants. We evaluated the incidence and prevalence of EoE over time in Canton of Vaud, Switzerland. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Canton of Vaud lies in the French-speaking, Western part of Switzerland. As of December 2013, it had a population of 743,317 inhabitants. We contacted all pathology institutes (n = 6) in this canton to identify patients that have been diagnosed with esophageal eosinophilia between 1993 and

2013. We then performed a chart review in all adult and pediatric gastroenterology practices to identify patients with EoE. RESULTS: Of 263 patients with esophageal eosinophilia, a total of 179 fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for EoE. Median diagnostic delay was 4 (IQR 1-9) years. No patient was diagnosed with EoE prior to 2003. Incidence of EoE increased from 0.16/100,000 inhabitants in 2004 to 6.3/100,000 inhabitants in 2013 (P < 0.001). The cumulative EoE prevalence in 2013 was 24.1/100,000. The incidence in males was 2.8 times higher (95% CI 2.01-3.88, P < 0.001) when compared to that in females. The annual EoE incidence was 10.6 times higher (95%-CI 7.61-14.87, P <

0.001) in the period from 2010 to 2013 when compared to that in the period from 1993 to 2009. CONCLUSIONS: The incidence and cumulative prevalence of EoE in Canton of Vaud, Switzerland, has rapidly increased in the past 10 years. © 2015 John Wiley & Sons A/S. Gastroenterology. 2014 May;146(5):1426-7. doi: 10.1053/j.gastro.2014.03.042. BACKGROUND & AIMS: Development of strictures is a major concern for patients with eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). At diagnosis, EoE can present with an inflammatory phenotype (characterized by whitish exudates, furrows, and edema), a stricturing phenotype (characterized by rings and stenosis), or a combination of these. Little is known about progression of stricture formation; we evaluated stricture development over time in the absence of treatment and investigated risk factors for stricture formation.

METHODS: We performed a retrospective study using the Swiss EoE Database, collecting data on 200 patients with symptomatic EoE (153 men; mean age at diagnosis, 39 ± 15 years old). Stricture severity was graded based on the degree of difficulty associated with passing of the standard adult endoscope. RESULTS: The median delay in diagnosis of EoE was 6 years (interquartile range,

2-12 years). With increasing duration of delay in diagnosis, the prevalence of fibrotic features of EoE, based on endoscopy, increased from 46.5% (diagnostic delay, 0-2 years) to 87.5% (diagnostic delay, >20 years; P = .020). Similarly, the prevalence of esophageal strictures increased with duration of diagnostic delay, from 17.2% (diagnostic delay, 0-2 years) to 70.8% (diagnostic delay, >20 years; P < .001). Diagnostic delay was the only risk factor for strictures at the time of EoE diagnosis (odds ratio = 1.08; 95% confidence interval: 1.040-1.122; P < .001).

CONCLUSIONS: The prevalence of esophageal strictures correlates with the duration of untreated disease. These findings indicate the need to minimize delay in diagnosis of EoE. BACKGROUND & AIMS: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a rapidly emerging, chronic inflammatory disorder. Prolonged inflammation evokes structural alterations and a fragile esophageal wall prone to perforation/rupture and food impaction. This report assesses the risk of spontaneously arising and procedure-induced complications and proposes practical recommendations.

METHODS: The Swiss Esophageal Esophagitis Database documented 251 confirmed cases. A chart review identified which patients had required endoscopic bolus removal and/or experienced transmural esophageal perforation/rupture. In addition, a MEDLINE search for "eosinophilic esophagitis" with "esophageal perforation" or "esophageal rupture" was undertaken. RESULTS: During an 18-year period, 87 patients (34.7%) experienced 134 food impactions requiring flexible (124, 92.5%) or rigid (10, 7.5%) endoscopic bolus removal. Transmural perforation occurred in 20% (2/10) of rigid procedures, and 1 esophageal rupture (Boerhaave's syndrome) was observed.

CONCLUSIONS: Bolus removal by rigid endoscopy is a high-risk procedure and should be avoided in eosinophilic esophagitis patients who require a gentler approach. Whether food impaction and esophageal wall remodeling can be prevented with anti-inflammatory medication is still undetermined. All Boerhaave's syndrome cases should be evaluated for underlying eosinophilic esophagitis. DOI: 10.1016/j.cgh.2008.02.003 PMID: 18407800 [Indexed for MEDLINE]

BACKGROUND: Oesophageal dilation is frequently used as an adjunct treatment to alleviate symptoms that develop from fibrostenotic remodelling in eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE). Earlier reports described an increased risk of complications associated with dilation.

AIM: Perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the efficacy and safety of endoscopic dilation in children and adults with EoE. METHODS: Professional librarians searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane library, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles in any language describing studies of dilation in EoE through December 2016. Studies were selected and data were abstracted independently and in duplicate. Random effects modelling was used to generate summary estimates for clinical improvement and complications (haemorrhage, perforation, hospitalisation, and death).

RESULTS: The search resulted in 3495 references, of which 27 studies were included in the final analysis. The studies described 845 EoE patients, including 87 paediatric patients, who underwent a total of 1820 oesophageal dilations. The median number of dilations was 3 (range: 1-35). Clinical improvement occurred in 95% of patients (95% CI: 90%-98%, I2 : 10%, 17 studies). Perforation occurred in 0.38% (95% CI: 0.18%-0.85%, I2 : 0%, 27 studies), haemorrhage in 0.05% (95% CI: 0%-0.3%, I2 : 0%, 18 studies), and hospitalisation in 0.67% (95% CI: 0.3%-1.1%, I2 : 44%, 24 studies). No deaths occurred (95% CI: 0%-0.2% I2 : 0%, 25 studies).

CONCLUSIONS: Endoscopic dilation is consistently effective in children and adults with EoE, resulting in improvement in 95% of patients with very low rates (<1%) of major complications. © 2017 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. DOI: 10.1111/apt.14123 PMID: 28513085 [Indexed for MEDLINE]

Electronic address: chudk@mcmaster.ca. BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic immune-mediated disease characterized by esophageal dysfunction and eosinophilic inflammation.

Comparative efficacy and safety of therapies remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To compare efficacy and safety of treatments for EoE in children and adults. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing pharmacologic, dietary, and mechanical interventions. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL to March 17, 2026. Reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. We conducted random-effects NMA; assessed certainty using GRADE.

RESULTS: We included 48 RCTs (3,963 participants). High-frequency dupilumab [mean difference (MD) -11.08, 95% confidence interval (CI) -15.14 to -7.03; high certainty] and swallowed topical corticosteroids (STCs) (MD -6.86, 95%CI -9.17 to -4.56; moderate certainty) are likely among the most effective for symptoms.

Similarly, high-frequency dupilumab (MD 6.57, 95%CI 3.42 to 9.71; moderate certainty) and STCs (MD 7.20, 95%CI 1.01 to 13.39; moderate certainty) are among the most effective for quality-of-life. Certain biologics and epicutaneous immunotherapy are likely not different from placebo for symptoms (moderate certainty). Multiple interventions reduce peak eosinophil counts (high certainty) and likely do not increase harms versus placebo (moderate or high certainty). Four- and six-food elimination diets (FEDs) may be better than 1FED for symptoms (low certainty), but not other outcomes, with greater burden.

CONCLUSIONS: High-frequency dupilumab and STCs are among the most effective therapies across patient-important and inflammatory outcomes. Histologic improvements do not guarantee patient-important outcome improvement. FED benefits are modest and low certainty, and traded off by burdens. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc. INTRODUCTION: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, antigen-driven inflammatory disease characterized by esophageal dysfunction and tissue remodeling. Despite increasing prevalence, its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. This review aims to systematically synthesize current evidence on the immunological, genetic, epithelial, and extracellular matrix mechanisms driving EoE. The goal is to identify upstream molecular targets and biomarkers to support precision medicine approaches.

METHODS: A PRISMA-based systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published between January 2014 and June 2025. Eligibility criteria were defined using the PECOS model, focusing on studies reporting quantitative biomolecular data. Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools for observational, in vivo , and in vitro studies. A total of 103 original research articles were included and categorized into 4 mechanistic domains.

RESULTS: The review identified epithelial barrier dysfunction, type 2 inflammation, and fibroblast activation as central features of EoE. Key cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TSLP) and transcriptional regulators (e.g., GATA-binding protein 3, Krüppel-like factor 5, resistin-like molecule alpha) were implicated in disease progression. Genetic and epigenetic analyses revealed susceptibility loci and persistent molecular alterations. Novel therapeutic targets and biomarkers were proposed, including TSLPR + pathogenic memory T-helper type 2A (Th2A) cells, lymphotoxin-like exhibits inducible expression competes with herpes simplex virus glycoprotein D for herpesvirus entry mediator a receptor expressed by T lymphocytes–herpesvirus entry mediator (LIGHT–HVEM) axis, and cluster of differentiation 73/ecto-5′-nucleotidase metabolic checkpoints.

DISCUSSION: EoE is a multifactorial disease involving complex immune–epithelial–stromal interactions. This review highlights emerging molecular pathways and supports a shift toward biomarker-guided, stratified treatment strategies. Integration of multiomics data and age-stratified analyses enhances understanding of disease heterogeneity. Future research should focus on longitudinal studies, pediatric cohorts, and validation of noninvasive biomarkers.

Over the last decades, the epidemiology of EoE has shown an increasing trend, with current prevalence estimated of up to 1 of 1,000 individuals in Western countries, with higher incidence peaks in male patients aged 35–39 years ( 2 ). EoE is considered an atopy-associated disorder, accordingly, more than half of patients with EoE exhibit at least one TH2-mediated allergic comorbidity ( 1 ).

Esophageal eosinophilia is the hallmark of EoE; indeed, current diagnostic criteria include an intraepithelial eosinophil peak count greater than or equal to 15 per high power fields in association with symptoms suggestive of EoE ( 2 , 3 ). Management of EoE includes elimination diets, orodispersible budesonide, and the off-label use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), as well as dupilumab—the only biologic therapy currently approved for EoE—alongside endoscopic dilation when fibrostenotic complications are present ( 2 ).

Recent evidence has contributed to significant advances in the understanding of the pathophysiology of EoE. Nevertheless, significant gaps still remain ( 4 ). Genetic susceptibility plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of EoE and impaired epithelial barrier function, which results in enhanced permeability to antigens that trigger the inflammatory response ( 5 , 6 ). The downstream self-maintaining inflammatory cascade is driven by Th2 response characterized by cytokine milieu that promote eosinophilic infiltration and tissue remodeling, which can ultimately lead to disease progression toward fibrostenotic phenotype ( 7 , 8 ). Despite the central role of eosinophils, accumulating evidence suggest that other immune cells, both innate and adaptive, and eosinophils-independent molecular pathways also contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease ( 4 ). Consistently, multiple biologic agents targeting eosinophils—anti IL-5 and Sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin 8—have proven efficacy in reducing tissue eosinophilia. However, they failed to achieve significant symptomatic improvement ( 9 – 11 ). This finding suggests that suppression of eosinophilic inflammation alone may be insufficient to achieve adequate disease control. Accordingly, dupilumab, the only biologic agent approved for the treatment of EoE, targets IL-4Rα, thus blocking both eosinophils-dependent and -independent IL-4- and IL-13–related pathways ( 12 ). Another critical issue is the absence of validated biomarker for disease monitoring, along with the lack of predictive factors for treatment response or failure. Therefore, in-depth exploration of EoE immunopathogenetic mechanism is crucial because it offers the possibility of identifying novel therapeutic targets located upstream in the pathogenetic mechanism and reliable biomarkers and predictive indicators, ultimately leading toward precision medicine.

METHODS This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines ( 13 ). The protocol was developed based on standards for mechanistic reviews addressing disease pathogenesis.

Eligibility criteria Given the focus on biological mechanisms, the PECOS model (Population, Exposure, Comparator Outcome, Study design) was used for eligibility criteria (see Supplementary Table S1, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). The article search was based on the keywords: “eosinophilic esophagitis,” “eosinophilic esophagitis,” “pathogenesis,” “cytokines,” “immune response,” “IL-5,” “IL-13,” “TSLP,” “tight junction,” “epithelial barrier,” “fibroblasts,” “extracellular matrix,” “barrier dysfunction,” “extracellular matrix.” Articles without molecular outcome measures were not included in the research. The detail description of records search can be found in Supplementary Material (see Supplementary Text S1, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ).

Only observational and experimental research articles were included in this study, while reviews (including systematic reviews), book chapters, meta-analyses, comments, and letters were excluded. Studies from conference proceedings or gray literature were also excluded. The selected studies provide original data collected through direct observation or experimentation, which is essential for drawing independent conclusions and performing quantitative synthesis.

The focus of this study was on observational and experimental research with direct participation of humans (e.g., cohort studies, case-control studies). Moreover, animal models of EoE, as well as in vitro and in vivo studies using human and/or animal tissues and/or cells were included in this investigation.

Articles that met the following criteria were analyzed in our review: (i) epidemiological studies investigating at least one of the following EoE indices: membrane or cytoplasm proteins, nuclei acids, immunoglobulins, cytokines, eosinophils, basophils, interleukins, mast cells (MC); (ii) studies evaluating animal models of EoE; (iii) studies analyzing cell cultures deriving from humans with EoE and/or animal models of EoE; (iv) computational studies analyzing genetic data of EoE patients and healthy controls; (v) studies reporting quantitative measures of EoE representative biomolecules; (vi) studies written in English.

All selected studies focused on immune, epithelial, genetic, or extracellular matrix (ECM) pathways in EoE. Among observational studies with the participation of humans, only studies quantifying the biomolecules difference between patients with EoE and subjects without EoE were considered. This study focused on the immune, epithelial, genetic, or ECM pathways leading to EoE development and progression. Thus, only articles presenting high-quality data on biomolecules variability as an effect of EoE were selected for this systematic review.

More elucidations on exclusion criteria are presented in the supplementary material (see Supplementary Text S2, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). Information sources A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for articles published in English from January 1, 2014, to June 1, 2025. All study designs were eligible, including human, animal, and in vitro experimental studies.

The literature search was restricted to studies published from January 2014 onward. This starting point was chosen because the years 2014–2015 marked the emergence of several landmark mechanistic discoveries—such as the identification of calpain 14 (CAPN14), the characterization of IL-13–driven epithelial remodeling, and the first genome-wide risk loci for EoE—that fundamentally reshaped the conceptual and molecular framework of the disease. These studies introduced modern approaches to understanding epithelial barrier dysfunction, Th2-mediated inflammation, and genetic susceptibility, and collectively established the basis for contemporary mechanistic research in EoE. Earlier publications generally lacked multiomics methodologies and did not consistently report biomolecular endpoints relevant to our review. Selecting 2014 as the lower bound therefore ensured that the included literature reflects current experimental standards and mechanistic perspectives.

Search strategy The search strategy was based on the keywords: “eosinophilic esophagitis,” “eosinophilic esophagitis,” “pathogenesis,” “cytokines,” “immune response,” “IL-5,” “IL-13,’ “TSLP,” “tight junction,” “epithelial barrier,” “fibroblasts,” “extracellular matrix,” “barrier dysfunction,” “extracellular matrix.” The detail description of records' search is presented in Supplementary Text S1 (see Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). All selected studies were published in English (language filter) between January 1, 2014, and June 1, 2024 (date range filter).

Study selection No automation tolls were used in the selection process. Four reviewers (J.L., A.D., S.F., and M.C.F) separately and independently screened the records gathered from the databases, assessing each record's eligibility based on titles, abstracts, and full texts when necessary.

Studies that satisfied the following criteria were included in this review: (i) epidemiological studies investigating at least one of the following EoE indices: membrane or cytoplasm proteins, nuclei acids, immunoglobulins, cytokines, eosinophils, basophils, interleukins, MC; (ii) studies evaluating animal models of EoE; (iii) studies analyzing cell cultures deriving from humans with EoE and/or animal models of EoE; (iv) computational studies analyzing genetic data of EoE patients and healthy controls; (v) studies reporting quantitative measures of EoE representative biomolecules; (vi) studies written in English.

Four reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts. Conflicts were resolved via discussion of all 4 reviewers. The PRISMA flow diagram summarizes the selection process. Data items and data collection process A standardized extraction sheet was used to collect the following data: (i) author(s), (ii) year, (iii) country, (iv) study design, (v) experimental models, (vi) population size, (vii) molecular targets investigated, (viii) main mechanistic results.

Quality and risk-of-bias assessment The quality of included studies was independently assessed by 4 reviewers using 3 different tools based on study type: the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) for human observational studies, the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) Risk of Bias tool for animal experiments, and a custom checklist for in vitro studies. Discrepancies in scoring were resolved through discussion or by involving a fifth reviewer.

For clinical observational studies, we used the NOS, a validated tool widely used to assess the quality of non-randomized studies in meta-analyses ( 14 ). This scale evaluates 3 main domains: Selection of study groups, Comparability of groups, and Outcome assessment. The maximum score is 9 stars for cohort and case-control designs and 7 stars for cross-sectional studies. According to established thresholds ( 15 ), studies were considered of good quality if they received 3–4 stars in Selection, 1–2 in Comparability, and 2–3 in Outcome; fair quality if they scored 2 in Selection, 1–2 in Comparability, and 2–3 in Outcome; poor quality if they received 0–1 in Selection, 0 in Comparability, or 0–1 in Outcome.

Animal studies were assessed using the SYRCLE's Risk of Bias tool ( 16 ), an adaptation of the Cochrane tool for animal research. This tool comprises 10 domains evaluating bias across 6 categories: selection bias (e.g., random sequence generation, allocation concealment), performance bias (e.g., random housing, blinding of personnel), detection bias (e.g., blinding of outcome assessors), attrition bias, reporting bias, and other potential biases. Each domain was judged as “low,” “high,” or “unclear” risk of bias.

For in vitro studies, a structured quality assessment was conducted using a custom checklist developed for this review. The checklist was based on widely accepted standards for robust cell-based experiments and included 6 criteria: Cell line origin and characterization (e.g., source, authentication), experimental design clarity (e.g., defined interventions and timepoints), inclusion of replicates (biological and/or technical), use of appropriate controls (positive/negative), methodological transparency (detailed protocol), statistical rigor (use of appropriate tests and sample size justification). Each study was assessed across all 6 domains, with those fulfilling all criteria considered at low risk of bias.

In several studies included in this review, the number of participants, animals, or experimental replicates was either incompletely reported or not specified. To ensure consistency in our quality evaluation, missing sample size information was handled according to the requirements and scoring structures of the specific risk-of-bias tools applied. For observational human studies assessed with the NOS, sample size is not an explicit scoring domain; however, when the absence of sample size reporting affected the interpretability of selection or outcome adequacy, the corresponding items were conservatively judged as “unclear” rather than “low risk.” For animal studies evaluated using the SYRCLE tool, lack of sample size reporting contributed to an “unclear risk” rating in domains related to selection bias, performance bias, or detection bias when the missing information prevented full assessment of allocation, housing conditions, or outcome measurement reliability. In vitro studies assessed with our custom methodological checklist were similarly scored as “unclear” in the relevant criteria (e.g., replicates and methodological transparency) when sample size or replicate details were not provided.

Across all study types, missing sample size information therefore did not result in automatic exclusion but was incorporated into the risk-of-bias judgement by reducing confidence in the affected domains. This approach ensured that uncertainty arising from incomplete reporting was explicitly reflected in the overall assessment while maintaining inclusion of mechanistically informative studies central to this review.

Sensitivity analysis We made the analyses to evaluate the eventual causes of heterogeneity and examined the robustness of the outcome evaluations: (i) We limited our analyses to biomolecules qualitative and quantitative analysis between models with and without EoE. (ii) We independently analyzed data collected in observational studies (adults and pediatrics separately), in vivo animal models and in vitro cellular studies. (iii) In all data elaborations, we chose the outcome estimate that had the highest significance for each study group and showed a significant difference between samples with and without EoE characteristics.

Effect measures The effect outcomes presented as quantitative and qualitative analysis of biomolecules, which significantly differs between models with and without EoE were taken from the original manuscript. Synthesis methods The synthesis of findings was structured around 4 mechanistic domains relevant to EoE: (i) innate and adaptive immunity, (ii) genetic and epigenetic mechanisms, (iii) ECM remodeling, and (iv) transcription factors and other regulatory proteins. Studies were grouped according to their biological focus and experimental model (human observational, in vivo animal, or in vitro cellular), allowing for stratified analysis across systems and age groups.

Quantitative and qualitative data on biomolecular markers were extracted and compared between EoE and non-EoE models. The synthesis emphasized molecular targets with consistent differential expression, functional relevance, and therapeutic potential. Where applicable, convergence across multiple studies was highlighted using visual tools (e.g., Venn diagrams) to identify shared gene signatures and pathway-level insights. This approach enabled a comprehensive mechanistic mapping of EoE pathogenesis, integrating multiomics data and identifying candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets across diverse experimental contexts.

Study characteristics The pathomechanisms of EoE can be divided into 4 main pathways, for instance, innate and adaptive immunity mechanisms, genetic driven mechanisms, ECM-related pathways, and transcription factors together with other protein-related pathways. Thus, 103 selected records were analyzed in these 4 categories. Innate and adaptive immunity pathway was analyzed on the base of 69 records, among which 14 records presenting data on epithelial barrier dysfunction, 39 records presenting data on innate immune cells and cytokines, and 16 records describing the recent findings on the role of adaptive immunity in EoE.

Genetic basis of EoE were analyzed based on 21 records relative to genetic risk loci and polymorphism (2 records), epigenetic alternations (2 records), and multiomics and transcriptomics approaches (17 records). There were 8 records describing ECM involvement in EoE, and 5 articles presenting role of other proteins and transcription factors in EoE. The analysis was made on records presenting data collected during observational studies (65 research studies on adults and 11 studies on pediatric patients), in vivo models (22 records), and in vitro cellular studies using cells derived from human or animal biopsies (50 records).

Heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses Given the methodological diversity of the included studies—spanning human observational cohorts, in vivo models, and in vitro mechanistic experiments—addressing heterogeneity was essential to ensure interpretability and robustness of the findings. To systematically manage variability across study types, we performed a series of planned sensitivity and subgroup analyses that stratified the evidence according to key biological and methodological dimensions.

First, observational clinical studies were analyzed separately for adult and pediatric populations. This distinction reduced age-related heterogeneity in epithelial, immunologic, and transcriptomic profiles and enabled clearer identification of convergent mechanistic pathways shared across life stages. Second, in vivo animal models were synthesized independently from clinical studies to avoid cross-species variability influencing overall mechanistic interpretations. Third, in vitro cellular studies were evaluated as a distinct evidence layer, recognizing the controlled but highly reductionist nature of cell-based systems and allowing their molecular insights (e.g., cytokine signaling, epithelial remodeling, and fibroblast activation) to be interpreted without conflation with whole-organism findings. Fourth, within preclinical work, we further distinguished between human-derived and animal-derived primary tissues, allowing us to assess the consistency of epithelial and stromal responses across species and experimental platforms.

These structured subgroup analyses helped reduce methodological heterogeneity by ensuring that mechanistic signals were evaluated within biologically coherent categories. This approach also revealed strong convergence across systems: epithelial barrier disruption, IL-13–driven inflammation, fibroblast reprogramming, and ECM alterations emerged consistently across adult and pediatric cohorts, across in vivo and in vitro models, and across human-derived and animal-derived tissues. Such cross-model alignment strengthened confidence in the robustness and generalizability of the mechanistic pathways identified.

Despite these efforts, formal meta-analytic subgroup analysis was not feasible. The mechanistic nature of the included evidence—characterized by diverse biomolecular endpoints, variable assay platforms, distinct experimental designs, and heterogeneous reporting formats—precluded the identification of shared quantitative effect measures necessary for meta-analytic pooling. Because studies frequently reported fold-changes, qualitative molecular patterns, or pathway-level results rather than standardized numerical outcomes, statistical aggregation would have been inappropriate and potentially misleading.

Nonetheless, our stratified narrative synthesis allowed us to address heterogeneity as systematically as possible. By isolating sources of biological and methodological variation and synthesizing evidence within comparable subgroups, we were able to identify coherent mechanistic themes while preserving the integrity of the diverse data types included in this review. Future mechanistic research would benefit from standardized reporting of quantitative molecular outcomes, which could enable more formal comparative analyses and quantitative integration across studies.

Risk of bias assessment analysis The risk of bias across the included studies was assessed using domain-specific tools: the NOS for observational clinical studies, the SYRCLE Risk of Bias tool for animal models, and a customized checklist tailored to in vitro experiments. Overall, the methodological quality was acceptable, although certain limitations—particularly in preclinical studies—warrant attention.

Clinical studies The observational clinical studies showed consistently high methodological quality according to the NOS, with total scores ranging from 7 to 9 out of a maximum of 9 stars. All studies were judged to be at low risk of bias. The strongest domains included the representativeness of the exposed cohort, the adequacy of the control group, and the ascertainment of exposure. The most common source of uncertainty was related to follow-up duration and adequacy, which was not always clearly described.

Animal studies. The quality of the animal studies, assessed using the SYRCLE Risk of Bias tool, was generally moderate, with all studies categorized as having a moderate risk of bias. A particularly consistent and concerning issue was the lack of information on random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding procedures—all of which were systematically either unreported or explicitly absent. These limitations introduce substantial risks of selection, performance, and detection bias. This issue is not isolated: According to a large-scale analysis of preclinical studies, up to 87% failed to implement random allocation and 86% did not use blinding, despite SYRCLE's explicit inclusion of these domains as critical quality criteria ( 29 ). While outcome data were generally complete and selective reporting was low, the lack of methodological safeguards significantly limits the internal validity and translational potential of the findings.

In vitro studies. In vitro experiments were evaluated with a custom risk of bias checklist developed for this review. These studies were uniformly judged to be at low risk of bias. All fulfilled the 6 methodological criteria, including detailed cell line characterization, clear experimental design, inclusion of replicates, appropriate use of controls, transparent methodology, and rigorous statistical analysis. The clarity and reproducibility of the protocols substantially increase the reliability of these findings.

Taken together, the studies included in this review present a methodologically robust foundation for our analysis. However, the systematic absence of randomization and blinding in animal studies represents a notable limitation that could affect the internal validity of preclinical findings. Improved reporting and implementation of these methodological safeguards in future studies will be essential to enhance the translational value of animal models in gastrointestinal research.

Results of individual studies Innate and adaptive immunity in eosinophilic esophagitis. Epithelial barrier dysfunction Among the studies analyzed, 8 were experimental translational investigations using in vitro and/or in vivo models, 6 of which also included patient-derived samples, while 6 were purely clinical case-control studies based on esophageal biopsies (see Supplementary Table S2a, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). Despite these differences, a consistent theme emerges: Epithelial barrier dysfunction plays a pivotal role in EoE pathogenesis.

Rather than being a consequence of inflammation, barrier disruption actively contributes to disease onset. Structural junctional proteins are among the most affected. Desmoglein-1 (DSG1) is consistently reduced in EoE, compromising epithelial cohesion and promoting periostin deposition ( 30 , 31 ). IL-13–induced CAPN14 specifically degrades DSG1, exacerbating barrier loss ( 32 ). Tight junction proteins are similarly affected: Claudin-7 and filaggrin (FLG) are reduced by transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β1) and IL-13, respectively, increasing permeability ( 33 , 34 ). Involucrin downregulation further suggests impaired epithelial maturation ( 35 ). Reduced E-cadherin and zonula occludens 1 expression, together with nuclear β-catenin and Twist1 activation, indicate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), contributing to remodeling and fibrosis ( 36 ).

Differentiation and cytoskeletal regulators further link cytokine signaling to epithelial remodeling. Synaptopodin (SYNPO), upregulated by IL-13, impairs epithelial motility and barrier integrity ( 19 ). Resistin-like molecule alpha (RELM-α) promotes epithelial hyperplasia and basal layer thickening, driving CD4 + T cell and eosinophil accumulation ( 37 ), while bone morphogenetic protein-driven nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 signaling regulates epithelial differentiation; its inhibition by follistatin induces basal cell hyperplasia ( 38 ).

Protease and inflammatory pathways also contribute to epithelial injury. Kallikrein-related peptidase 5 (KLK5) activates protease-activated receptor 2, promoting inflammation and barrier breakdown, whereas its inhibition reduces eosinophilia ( 39 ). Krüppel-like factor 4-driven Ras homolog family member F (RHOF) and nuclear factor kappa B activation in keratinocytes induces epithelial inflammation and remodeling ( 40 ). Moreover, IL-4 stimulates the H + ,K + -ATPase in epithelial cells, leading to calcium-dependent eotaxin-3 secretion and enhanced eosinophil recruitment, an effect reversed by PPIs or calcium-channel blockade ( 26 ).

Metabolic regulation plays an additional role. Loss of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha signaling shifts epithelial metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation and impairs differentiation, whereas its stabilization restores glycolysis and barrier integrity ( 41 ). Collectively, these findings support a model where early structural and metabolic dysregulation of epithelial cells facilitates antigen penetration and chronic inflammation. Targeting epithelial differentiation programs, protease activity, and metabolic reprogramming may represent promising therapeutic approaches to restore mucosal integrity and prevent disease progression in EoE.

Innate immune cells and cytokines Of the studies examined, 22 were experimental translational investigations using in vitro and/or in vivo models, 16 of which also incorporated patient-derived samples, whereas 17 were purely clinical case-control or retrospective studies based on human biopsies or blood specimens (see Supplementary Table S2b, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). Models ranged from human biopsies, blood, and serum to genetically modified mice and epithelial cell lines, covering pediatric and adult cohorts and comparisons with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and celiac disease.

Epithelial-derived alarmins, IL-33, IL-18, and TSLP, initiate type 2 inflammation. IL-33 promotes eosinophilia through IL-5 and IL-13, while IL-18 activates invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells to produce IL-5/IL-13, driving mast cell accumulation and fibrosis ( 42 – 44 ). Peripheral iNKT cells show reduced frequency and increased low-affinity immunoglobulin E receptor II expression, suggesting tissue homing and biomarker potential ( 45 ). Dysregulation of noncanonical nuclear factor kappa B signaling also amplifies epithelial inflammation ( 46 ). TSLP bridges innate and adaptive immunity by activating TSLPR + CD4 + T cells through STAT5 signaling, enhancing IL-5 and IL-13 production ( 47 ).

MC and eosinophils act as central effector cells. MC persist during remission, releasing IL-13 and oncostatin M that weaken epithelial junctions and perpetuate inflammation ( 48 – 50 ). Histamine receptor signaling (H1R, H2R, H4R) enhances epithelial cytokine release ( 51 ), while vasoactive intestinal peptide–chemoattractant receptor-homologous molecule expressed on T-helper type 2 cells signaling couples mast cell and eosinophil activation, contributing to dysmotility ( 23 ).

Eosinophils are sustained by IL-5, IL-33, and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF)–C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 signaling ( 22 , 43 ) and regulated by inhibitory mechanisms such as paired immunoglobulin-like receptor B (PIR-B) ( 25 ). They mediate cytotoxicity ( 52 ).

Macrophage-derived colony-stimulating factor 1 promotes fibrosis, epithelial proliferation, and ECM remodeling ( 53 ), while stem cell factor enhances eosinophilia and Th2 cytokine production ( 24 ). IL-13 and its receptor interleukin-13 receptor alpha 1 (IL-13Rα1) drive epithelial proliferation and fibrotic remodeling ( 18 ), and high IL-5/IL-13 levels distinguish EoE from celiac disease ( 54 ). Long-term control of eosinophilia reduces fibrostenotic risk ( 55 ).

Beyond Th2 circuits, interferon γ (IFN-γ) from CD8 + resident memory T cells disrupts epithelial integrity ( 27 ). Forkhead box P3 Tregs expand during active disease but decline in remission, indicating dynamic immune adaptation. Recent transcriptomic data revealed downregulation of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2 and an inverse correlation with Treg markers, suggesting a dysregulated neutrophil–Treg axis sustaining chronic inflammation ( 56 ).

In summary, epithelial alarmins orchestrate innate and adaptive immune responses, driving eosinophilic inflammation and tissue remodeling. Key therapeutic targets include IL-13Rα1, TSLP–STAT5, interleukin-18/NLR family pyrin domain-containing protein 3, MIF–CXCR4, and stem cell factor. Supplementary Figure S1 (see Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ) presents a color-coded diagram of these immunological pathways.

Adaptive immunity in eosinophilic esophagitis To explore the contribution of adaptive immunity to EoE, 16 studies were reviewed (see Supplementary Table S2c, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). Nine adopted an experimental translational design integrating in vitro and/or in vivo models, 6 of which also analyzed patient-derived samples, while 7 were purely clinical case-control or retrospective investigations based on esophageal biopsies or blood specimens. Together, these studies delineate how T cell–driven cytokine polarization, fibroblast activation, and impaired tolerance sustain chronic inflammation and remodeling in EoE.

Adaptive immunity drives chronicity in EoE through antigen-specific T-cell responses and type 2 cytokine polarization. IL-13 is a central mediator, activating STAT3/STAT6, inducing secreted frizzled-related protein 1, and promoting epithelial hyperplasia ( 57 ). It also regulates leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 31, which maintains barrier integrity; its loss worsens dysfunction and predicts poor treatment response ( 58 ). IL-4 enhances eotaxin-3 secretion through calcium and proton-pump pathways, amplifying eosinophil recruitment ( 26 ).

Wright et al ( 59 ) demonstrated increased GATA-binding protein 3 and T-bet expression in esophageal CD4 + T cells from patients with EoE and proton pump inhibitor-responsive esophageal eosinophilia (PPI-REE) compared with GERD and controls, with both markers decreasing after treatment, indicating shared T-helper type 1/T-helper type 2 activation patterns between EoE and PPI-REE.

Th2 cytokines also promote stromal remodeling: IL-9 and granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor activate MC and myeloid cells ( 60 ), while suppression of tumorigenicity 2 Th2 cells produce amphiregulin in response to IL-33, stimulating fibroblasts and collagen deposition ( 61 ). TSLPR + memory CD4 + Th2A cells, activated through TSLP–STAT5 signaling, produce IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-9 in a feed-forward loop ( 47 ). Their frequency correlates with eosinophilia and disease severity, making them a biomarker and therapeutic target.

Beyond Th2 pathways, IFN-γ, secreted by CD8 + tissue-resident memory T cells, disrupts epithelial proliferation and tight junctions, inducing apoptosis ( 27 ). Plasmacytoid dendritic cells may amplify this through type I interferons. These findings reveal a non-Th2 axis contributing to epithelial damage and chronic inflammation ( 62 ).

Forkhead box P3 regulatory T cells (Tregs) normally suppress excessive immune responses and maintain tolerance. In EoE, Tregs are increased in the esophageal mucosa but show impaired function. Their numbers decline after histologic remission, indicating dynamic immune remodeling during disease progression and treatment ( 63 ). Compared with GERD, patients with EoE show reduced Treg induction, suggesting a failure of tolerance mechanisms that favors Th2-driven inflammation ( 64 ). IL-33 signaling may further suppress Treg activity, tipping the balance toward inflammation.

T follicular helper (TFH) cells contribute to humoral responses in EoE, which diverge from classical immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated food allergy. TFH IL-10 + cells promote immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) production, leading to local IgG4 deposition in esophageal tissue ( 28 ). This contrasts with TFH13-driven IgE responses seen in milk allergy. Esophageal CD4 + T cells produce IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-10, and IL-21, sustaining both inflammation and IgG4-mediated tissue changes.

Lymphotoxin-like, exhibits inducible expression, competes with herpes simplex virus glycoprotein D for herpesvirus entry mediator, a receptor expressed by T lymphocytes (LIGHT) or TNFSF14 (tumor necrosis factor superfamily member 14), produced by activated T cells, drives stromal remodeling in EoE. It induces an inflammatory phenotype in fibroblasts through intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1), promotes eosinophil adhesion, and synergizes with TGF-β1 to stimulate myofibroblast differentiation and collagen deposition ( 20 , 65 ). These findings link adaptive immune signals directly to fibrosis.

Adaptive immunity in EoE is dominated by IL-13–driven Th2 responses but also involves pathogenic memory Th2A cells, impaired Treg tolerance, non-Th2 interferon pathways, and TFH–B-cell circuits. This multifaceted immune landscape sustains chronic inflammation and fibrostenotic remodeling. Therapeutic strategies may target IL-13, TSLP, LIGHT–fibroblast interactions, and interferon-driven epithelial injury. Supplementary Figure S2 (see Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ) graphically summarizes the role of adaptive immunity in EoE.

The genetic basis of eosinophilic esophagitis. Twenty-one studies (see Supplementary Table S3, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ) were analyzed to assess the genetic basis of EoE. These include case-control designs, prospective trials, cohort studies, and computational analyses using large datasets. Sample types range from esophageal biopsies and blood leukocytes to extracellular vesicles and cell lines, with both pediatric and adult cohorts represented.

A wide array of molecular techniques was used, including RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), single-cell RNA-seq, microRNA (miRNA) profiling, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation, genome-wide association study, proteomics, and pathway analysis. Sample sizes varied from small cohorts (n = 18) to large-scale studies (n = 1,214), although most genome-wide association study cohorts were predominantly of European ancestry.

Key findings include altered expression of IL-13, periostin (POSTN), and C-C motif chemokine ligand 26 (CCL26) (eotaxin-3), epigenetic changes (e.g., CpG methylation), and dysregulated miRNAs (e.g., miR-155 and miR-375). Studies also revealed shifts in immune cell composition and microbiome alterations (e.g., Fusobacterium enrichment). Some focused on treatment response, while others explored genetic susceptibility and biomarker discovery.

Collectively, these studies highlight the role of genetic susceptibility in EoE, implicating pathways involved in epithelial barrier integrity, immune regulation, and allergic inflammation. The integration of transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic data provides a foundation for personalized approaches to diagnosis and therapy.

Genetic risk loci and polymorphisms Genetic studies have identified key EoE risk loci, notably at 16p13, involving C-type lectin domain family 16 member A, dexamethasone-induced protein, and class II major histocompatibility complex transactivator, with immune-cell-specific expression patterns ( 66 ). Variants in TSLP and toll-like receptor 3 suggest a pathogenic epithelial signaling axis ( 67 ). Rare damaging mutations in dehydrogenase E1 and transketolase domain-containing protein 1, oxoglutarate dehydrogenase-like protein, dedicator of cytokinesis 8 (DOCK8), and myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88 impair mitochondrial and immune functions, reinforcing the immune-genetic basis of EoE ( 68 ). These findings highlight the role of genetic susceptibility in epithelial barrier dysfunction, Th2 inflammation, and immune dysregulation, offering insights into disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets.

Epigenetic alterations Epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation also seem to modulate EoE pathogenesis. Methylation profiles of esophageal biopsies from patients with EoE—especially children—clearly separate them from healthy controls, even after first-line therapy, suggesting a lasting epigenetic imprint associated with disease ( 69 ). Another study confirmed that methylation differences are associated with treatment responsiveness, highlighting pathways related to cell adhesion, epithelial barrier integrity, and cellular aging ( 70 ).

Multiomics and transcriptomic approaches Differential gene expression in EoE has been explored using diverse methods, including single-cell RNA-seq ( 49 , 71 – 73 ), bulk RNA-seq ( 19 , 68 , 74 ), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) ( 71 , 75 ), microarrays ( 76 ), meta-transcriptomics ( 77 ), and miRNA profiling ( 78 – 80 ). These approaches reveal consistent upregulation of genes linked to inflammation and epithelial remodeling, such as POSTN, arachidonate 15-lipoxygenase, eosinophil peroxidase, and collagen type I alpha-2 chain.

Wen et al ( 81 ) further demonstrated that PPI-REE shares an EoE-like Th2 transcriptomic profile characterized by elevated CCL26, POSTN, carboxypeptidase A3, and DSG1 expression; PPI monotherapy normalized this signature and identified differential clusters (notably potassium inwardly rectifying channel subfamily J member 2) distinguishing PPI-REE from EoE.

Single-cell RNA-seq identified cell-type–specific expression of IL13, joining chain of multimeric immunoglobulins, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8, and fibroblast-associated signatures correlating with fibrosis ( 72 ). Rochman et al ( 47 ) found increased TSLP-responsive memory CD4 + T cells, supporting anti-TSLP therapy as a precision approach.

Keever-Keigher et al ( 73 ) profiled peripheral blood mononuclear cells across eosinophilic and inflammatory bowel disease conditions, identifying EGR1 as a key differentially expressed gene (DEG) in Th2 cells, upregulated by zinc. This links zinc dysregulation to eosinophilia and epithelial stress. miRNA studies revealed dysregulation of miR-203, miR-375, miR-21, and miR-223, with limited correlation to circulating levels ( 78 ). miRNAs in plasma-derived extracellular vesicles (e.g., miR-10b-5p and miR-125a-5p) were elevated in active EoE ( 79 ). miR-155 was shown to impair barrier integrity by targeting claudin 7 ( 80 ).

Comparative analysis of 8 adult EoE studies identified shared DEGs (Figure 2 a): apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme catalytic subunit 3A, epiplakin 1, DSG1, CCL26, solute carrier family 9 member A3, POSTN, IL1RL1, and C-C motif chemokine ligand 24. Cross-age comparisons (Figure 2 b) revealed 6 common DEGs in pediatric and adult EoE: joining chain of multimeric immunoglobulins, DSG1, POSTN, cadherin 1, cysteine-rich secretory protein 3, and CCL26. Figure 2. Venn diagram of ( a ) DE genes in selected studies on adult EoE biopsies and ( b ) DE genes in selected studies on pediatric and adult EoE biopsies. EoE, eosinophilic esophagitis.

These findings support a multiomics approach to understanding EoE and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. The main characteristics of DE genes presented in Figure 2 are described in Supplementary Table S6 (see Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ).

In line with current international consensus, PPI-REE is no longer regarded as a separate diagnostic entity but rather as part of the EoE continuum. This position, endorsed by the A Working Group on Proton Pump Inhibitor-Responsive Esophageal Eosinophilia (AGREE) conference and subsequent international guidelines, reflects accumulating evidence that PPI responsiveness represents a therapeutic phenotype rather than a distinct disease mechanism. Our findings further support this perspective: transcriptomic, immunologic, and molecular signatures reported in studies of PPI-responsive patients closely mirror those observed in classical EoE, including shared Th2-associated pathways, epithelial barrier alterations, and overlapping gene-expression profiles. These convergent mechanistic features reinforce the view that PPI-REE constitutes a phenotypic variant within the broader EoE spectrum, underscoring the importance of evaluating PPI response as a treatment attribute rather than a basis for differential diagnosis.

Extracellular matrix in esophagitis eosinophils. Over the past decade, 8 studies have investigated ECM remodeling in EoE, including 5 in vitro studies using fibroblasts from esophageal biopsies, 1 in vivo mouse model, and 2 pediatric biopsy-based studies (see Supplementary Table S5). These studies vary in design, sample type, and molecular focus, offering a broad view of ECM involvement in EoE pathogenesis.

Zdanowicz et al ( 82 ) examined matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 1 (TIMP-1) expression in pediatric EoE biopsies. TIMP-1 was absent in EoE but present in EoE and controls, suggesting a proteolytic imbalance favoring ECM degradation. Strong MMP-1 expression correlated with poor response to standard therapies, indicating its potential as a prognostic biomarker.

Clevenger et al ( 83 ) used single-cell RNA-seq to show that basal cell hyperplasia in EoE is driven by suprabasal epithelial cells retaining progenitor-like transcriptional programs. These cells overexpress SRY-box transcription factor 2 and Krüppel-like factor 5, fail to differentiate, and exhibit a wound-repair–like phenotype, distinct from GERD. This suggests chronic inflammation disrupts epithelial homeostasis through altered differentiation.

Baruch-Morgenstern et al ( 43 ) demonstrated that PIR-B, an inhibitory receptor on eosinophils, suppresses IL-13–induced remodeling in a mouse model. PIR-B deficiency led to increased eosinophil activation, epithelial hyperplasia, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis. Eosinophil depletion reversed these effects, confirming PIR-B's role in limiting tissue damage.

Fibroblasts have emerged as key ECM regulators in EoE. Studies show their functional plasticity and reprogramming under inflammatory conditions, contributing to fibrosis and structural remodeling. Together, these findings highlight ECM dysregulation as a central feature of EoE, linking immune activation to tissue remodeling and offering new therapeutic targets such as MMP-1, PIR-B, and epithelial differentiation pathways.

Five in vitro studies have explored fibroblast behavior in EoE using cells derived from human esophageal biopsies. Cheng et al ( 84 ) showed that IL-4/IL-13 stimulate eotaxin-3 via STAT6 in both epithelial cells and fibroblasts, contributing to inflammation and fibrosis. Janus kinase-STAT6 inhibitors block this effect, while PPIs act only on epithelial cells, suggesting limited impact on subepithelial fibrosis.

Muir et al ( 85 ) demonstrated that matrix stiffness and TGF-β synergistically drive fibroblast activation and myofibroblast differentiation, perpetuating fibrosis even in inactive disease. Li et al ( 86 ) identified 2 fibroblast subtypes: F_A (contractile) and F_B (ECM-depositing), with F_B dominant in active/remission EoE and enriched in EMT pathways. Jumabay et al ( 21 ) found EoE fibroblasts undergo pathogenic reprogramming, showing impaired adipogenesis, enhanced migration, and reduced cluster of differentiation 73/ecto-5′-nucleotidase (CD73) activity. Adenosine supplementation restored fibroblast function, suggesting a metabolic checkpoint.

Manresa et al ( 65 ) identified LIGHT (TNFSF14) as a T cell–derived cytokine that drives fibroblast differentiation into an inflammatory–myofibroblast hybrid. LIGHT upregulates ICAM-1, promoting eosinophil tethering and localized inflammation. Together, these studies reveal fibroblast heterogeneity and their central role in fibrosis, inflammation, and epithelial remodeling, highlighting therapeutic targets such as STAT6, CD73, and LIGHT.

Nonproteins and metabolic mediators. The role of nonprotein molecules and metabolites in EoE pathomechanisms has been explored in several studies (see Supplementary Table S6, Supplementary Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/CTG/B535 ). These investigations employ a variety of designs, from prospective clinical cohorts to in vitro epithelial models and analytical chemistry techniques. The sample types span esophageal mucosa (through impedance-pH), serum, and plasma, allowing assessment of mucosal integrity, systemic metabolic markers, and eosinophil activation signatures.

One of the most robust contributions comes from Frazzoni et al ( 87 ), who used impedance-pH monitoring in 60 patients with EoE (40 PPI-responsive, 20 PPI-refractory), 60 GERD, and 60 control subjects. They found that low mean nocturnal baseline impedance gradient between mid and distal esophagus predicts PPI refractoriness, and that postreflux swallow–induced peristaltic wave index distinguishes PPI-responder from nonresponder cases. These findings suggest that gastroesophageal reflux and impaired mucosal integrity may actively contribute to EoE pathogenesis and that part of PPI effectiveness may derive from improving chemical clearance and barrier properties.

At the epithelial and cellular level, Wheeler et al ( 88 ) explored the protective role of 17β-estradiol (E2) against IL-13–induced injury. In esophageal epithelial cell line 2 ALI esophageal epithelial cells, E2 pretreatment mitigated the loss of barrier function and remodeling effects by suppressing tyrosine kinase 2/STAT6 phosphorylation and restoring DSG1 expression, in an ESR2-dependent manner. This suggests a modulatory influence of sex hormones on EoE susceptibility and barrier integrity.

In the translational domain, Brusilovsky et al ( 89 ) examined vitamin D (25(OH)D 3 ) in pediatric EoE: They present evidence that vitamin D antagonizes IL-13–induced epithelial disruption and hyperproliferation, supporting barrier restoration. Cameron et al ( 90 ) then assessed serum 25(OH)D 3 in 40 EoE vs 40 non-EoE controls, finding lower mean levels in patients with EoE and an association between lower vitamin D and lamina propria fibrosis, although deficiency prevalence was similar.

Finally, Thomas et al ( 91 ) focused on 3-bromotyrosine (a marker of eosinophil activation) and L-tyrosine in plasma. They developed a sensitive liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) method and applied it to 4 patients with EoE, finding no clear correlation between plasma 3-bromotyrosine levels and eosinophil counts, although possible associations with esophageal structural changes were noted. This opens the possibility of noninvasive metabolic biomarkers for EoE activity.

Collectively, these studies hint that impedance metrics, hormonal modulation, vitamin D status, and eosinophil-derived metabolic byproducts may modulate or reflect EoE pathophysiology. However, most findings remain preliminary and require validation in larger cohorts and mechanistic models. Future research integrating multiomic biomarker panels (impedance, metabolomics, and hormonal assays) with histologic and clinical endpoints may reveal novel diagnostic or therapeutic pathways beyond the proteome.

DISCUSSION This systematic review builds on the foundational framework proposed by O'Shea et al ( 92 ), reinforcing the concept of EoE as a chronic, antigen-driven, type 2 immune-mediated disease marked by epithelial barrier dysfunction, eosinophilic inflammation, and progressive tissue remodeling. While O'Shea emphasized IL-13–induced CAPN14 expression and desmosomal protein degradation (e.g., DSG1 and FLG), our review identifies additional contributors to barrier disruption, including KLK5, SYNPO, and RELM-α, and highlights EMT and transcriptional reprogramming in suprabasal cells.
